scope: Navigation only. Each demo folder's metadata.json is the source; this file is generated and is never edited by hand. It records no validation or development state — run a folder's main.py to find out what works.

entries.title: AdamW step with BF16 state
entries.formula: m' = b1*m + (1-b1)*g; v' = b2*v + (1-b2)*g^2; p' = p*(1-lr*wd) - (lr/(1-b1^t)) * m'/(sqrt(v')/sqrt(1-b2^t) + eps); BF16 [1, N] state in and out, FP32 throughout the body
study_for: Where the precision boundary really is. Every state lives in BF16 in GM and the whole update runs in FP32 on chip: four `cast`s in, three `cast`s out, and nothing between them touches BF16. `state_reference` mirrors that exactly -- it computes in FP32 and calls `narrow_away` only at the three stores -- which is what makes a 2e-3 comparison a statement about one storage quantum instead of a guess.

The host owns the bias correction. `prepare_scalars` evaluates 1-lr*wd, lr/(1-b1^t) and 1/sqrt(1-b2^t) in Python binary64 and narrows each result to FP32 before the launch, so the device receives eight scalars in the fixed `SCALAR_NAMES` order and never evaluates a power, a reciprocal square root or a double. That order is part of the kernel signature, not a convention.

`narrow_away` encodes the BF16 word from FP32 bits as (magnitude + 0x8000) >> 16, which is nearest-ties-away, and it never calls Torch's own conversion. The `bf16_midpoints` case is what that buys: it builds one positive and one negative exact midpoint, and a reference written with `.bfloat16()` -- ties-to-even -- disagrees with the device on both of them.

`axpy(f_m, f_g, one_minus_beta1)` contracts a multiply and an add into one instruction while the reference writes `(m * beta1) + (g * one1)` as two. That seam, together with the tensor `div`, is the honest reason this unit has a tolerance at all; it is not a claim that the two round identically.
do_not_copy_when: You are trying to match an optimizer that keeps BF16 intermediates. This one narrows only at the three stores; an implementation that rounds after each step of the update disagrees with it by design, and widening the tolerance to hide that would hide a real defect instead.

You want one fused launch over many parameter tensors. Each tensor here is its own launch with its own `numel`, because every buffer is indexed at the same offset in all four inputs; a fused optimizer needs an offset table and a different partition.

You need the parameter updated in place. The kernel writes three separate destinations and aliases no input, which is exactly what lets the caller hand in NaN-poisoned tensors and detect a lane no core wrote; `p_update` is then computed on the host from the returned parameter.

entries.title: Dense document/anchor attention mask
entries.formula: mask[q, k] = doc[a(q)] >= 0 and doc[k] == doc[a(q)] and k < a(q) and (window < 0 or k >= a(q) - window) for k < T; mask[q, T+j] = blk(q) == blk(j) and (not causal or j <= q); a(q) is the anchor of q's block; uint8 [Q, T+Q] of exact 0/1
study_for: A Boolean answer computed with no comparison instruction. Every predicate is `sub`, then `vmaxs(_, 0.0)`, then `vmins(_, 1.0)`: the difference of two exact integers carried in FP32 clamps to exactly 0.0 or 1.0, and the predicates are combined with `mul` rather than a logical and. This is how an FP32 vector pipeline with no compare-to-mask produces a mask, and why the result can be compared bitwise rather than with a tolerance.

Two padding sentinels instead of a validity term. `metadata_for` marks key padding -2 and query padding -1, so the base test `1 - min(|doc_k - doc_q|, 1)` is already 0 for a padded query against a padded key -- the two sentinels can never be equal. One choice of constants deletes a whole term from the kernel, and a padded query still keeps its own synthetic block.

Reusing a buffer across loops, with the barrier that makes it legal. After `bar_all()` drains the base loop, the causal path reloads `ub_qdoc` and `ub_qdoc_b` -- the query-document rows -- with query indices built from the `kv_iota` ramp that is already in GM. The source comment above it states the argument. No extra UB buffer and no host-side mask are allocated for the causal mode at all.

The only route to a byte here is FP32 -> FP16 -> uint8, two `cast`s in a row. It is exact only because the FP32 side can hold nothing but 0.0 and 1.0; if a predicate ever produced 0.5 the byte cast would round it into a plausible-looking mask. main.py counts non-Boolean bytes in the result for exactly that reason, and compares as uint8 rather than as bool so a stray 2 cannot pass.
do_not_copy_when: Your predicate is not an integer comparison whose operands are exactly representable in FP32. The clamp trick needs the difference to be an exact integer; a fractional difference clamps to something strictly between 0 and 1 and the narrowing turns it into a wrong byte rather than an error.
T or Q is not a multiple of 64. The column loops walk whole TILE_N=64 chunks with no tail handling, and the five metadata rows are read at full tile width.

You want a sparse, blockwise or on-the-fly mask. This materializes a dense uint8[Q, T+Q] in global memory -- 8 MB per launch at the source shape -- which is the price it pays to make the consumer a plain indexed read.

entries.title: Eleven BF16 group-quantization formats
entries.formula: y = bf16(q(x/s) * s) per group, where s and q are the variant's policy: s = bf16(absmax/6) with the E2M1 grid or s = bf16(absmax/7) with a signed-int4 grid over a 16/32/64 group; s = floor_pow2(absmax32/4) for MXFP4, times a per-128 E0M8 macro factor for MBS; a per-32 private-exponent step for MXFP8 E5M2; a per-64 E6M2 scale with per-8 and per-4 exponent levels for HiFX 4/5; contiguous BF16 [rows, cols] in and out
study_for: Eleven entries behind one signature, with the launch mode recorded per entry instead of assumed. `ENTRIES` in kernel.py maps each entry to `vec` or `mix`: the MX bodies are vector launches, while the group and HiFX bodies were written as MIX launches whose cube side does no arithmetic at all. Nothing else about a case changes when you switch variants, so the eleven are directly comparable.

The grid and the scale policy are separate choices, and this folder is the controlled experiment. The same E2M1 magnitude grid appears under three different scales -- a BF16 absmax/6 in `group_scaled`, a floor-to-power-of-two E8M0 in `plain_mxfp4`, and that same E8M0 under a per-128 macro factor in `mbs_mxfp4` -- while `signed_int4_*` keeps a BF16 scale and swaps the grid for a clamped integer. Read the four references side by side before choosing either half for a new format.

Two different functions were called `quantize_abs_to_e2m1_g32` in two source modules. The one from mbs.py takes an explicit `rep_stride` because its rows are strided inside a 128-column macro tile; the one from group32 uses the default contiguous stride and is here as `quantize_abs_to_e2m1_g32_packed`. Separate files hid that they were not the same function, and a merge that let the later definition win would have silently changed the MXFP4 answer.

`mbs_mxfp4_tiny` preserves an FP32 overflow rather than repairing it: at absmax 2^-126 the macro factor's 6/absmax overflows to infinity, and the source then takes the top-8 mantissa bits of that infinity. reference.py reproduces it on purpose and says so in a comment. When a reconstruction is a contract with existing data, the bug is part of the contract.
do_not_copy_when: You are looking for FP4 E1M2. The `signed_int4_*` variants come from source files named e1m2, but they implement a signed integer grid clamped to [-8, 7] under a BF16 absmax/7 scale; using them as an E1M2 codec produces the wrong numbers with the right shape.

You need packed payload bytes or an externally shared scale. Every output here is a reconstructed BF16 value, and the E8M0 code, the E0M8 macro factor and the E6M2 scale are all internal numbers that are never published.
Your columns are not a multiple of the variant's group size. Groups never cross a logical row and there is no partial-group path; the tail these kernels handle is a partial tile of whole groups.
You only need the three MX formats in FP32. `grouped_fp32` is the shorter read: the same MXFP4, MBS and E5M2 policies without the group-size sweep or the BF16 store.

entries.title: Grouped FP32 formats: MXFP4, MBS-MXFP4, MXFP8 E5M2
entries.formula: plain_mxfp4: y = E2M1(x/s)*s with s = floor_pow2(amax32/4) >= 2^-127; mbs_mxfp4: f = 1 + top8(6/amax128)/256, y = plain_mxfp4(x*f)/f; mxfp8_e5m2: p = max(2^e_group * 2^-29, 2^e_x)/4 + 5.421011e-20, y = clip(round_half_away(x/p)*p, +-1.75*2^e_group); contiguous FP32 [rows, cols] in and out
study_for: How a per-group scale becomes one vector instruction. Each group's amax lands in a scalar slot of `[1, SCALE_SLOTS]`; `brcb` fans those 64 scalars out into 8-column blocks, and the following `div`/`mul` reads the broadcast with `src2_rep_stride=1` while the data side steps by `REP_F`. That stride pair is the whole trick -- 32 groups are normalized by 32 different scales in a single call, with no per-group loop.

The E8M0 scale is exponent-field arithmetic, not a rounding mode: `build_e8m0_scale_s` masks `FP32_EXP_MASK` out of amax/4 and clamps to `E8M0_MIN_VALUE` (2^-127), which is floor-to-power-of-two in two integer ops. `build_e0m8_macro_factor` does the complementary trick for MBS, taking the top eight mantissa bits of 6/amax to build 1 + k/256.

MBS is the plain format wrapped, not a new one. `mbs_mxfp4_kernel_fp32` multiplies the macro by its factor, calls the same per-32 E8M0/E2M1 body four times, then divides the factor back out -- the nesting is visible in the source as literal reuse of `quantize_abs_to_e2m1_g32`. Read `plain_mxfp4` first and MBS is one extra level.

`_a2_mbs_div` in reference.py is a host model of the A2 divider's tie behaviour, keyed on the macro factor's code and the dividend's mantissa. It exists because the final `div` by the macro factor lands exactly on a representable midpoint for a handful of factors, and a reference that used plain FP32 division disagreed on those elements. When a reconstruction reference needs a hardware rounding model, this is what it looks like.
do_not_copy_when: You need the packed payload. Every output here is a reconstructed FP32 value; the E8M0 scale and the E2M1 code are internal numbers that are never published, so none of this is a byte-level conversion ABI.

Your columns are not a multiple of the group size -- 32 for the MX formats, 128 for MBS. Groups never cross a logical row and there is no partial-group path; the tail these kernels handle is a partial tile of whole groups, which is a different thing.

You want a per-tensor or per-row quantizer. The schedule is sized around a group that fits one vector repeat: 64 scalar slots, an 8-column `brcb` block, a 32-group tile and a [33, 64] UB tile whose guard row and padding columns are private. A different group geometry re-tiles all of it.

entries.title: BF16 HiFloat8 quantize-dequantize
entries.formula: y = sign(x) * round_half_away(|x| / s) * s with s = 2^(e - m), e = floor(log2|x|), m = 3/2/1/0 as |e| <= 3/7/15/above; |x| >= 40960 -> +-inf, |x| < 2^-23 -> +0; contiguous BF16 [1, total] in and out
study_for: The quantization step is read out of the exponent field, not computed with a log. `_quantize_tile` masks FP32 bits with `FP32_EXP_MASK` to get 2^e, reflects that about the bias with `vnot` plus the `EXP_ABS_BIAS` add to get 2^|e|, then halves the scale once for each of the `le15_flag`/`le7_flag`/`le3_flag` compares. Three `select`s and three `mul`s replace the mantissa-width table the reference writes as nested `torch.where`.

Special values are computed, never branched on. Finite, overflow and NaN are three uint8 masks, and the published answer is the sum of three `select`ed terms — the quantized value, a restored signed infinity, and the restored non-finite input. Every lane executes the same instruction sequence, so there is no divergence for the scheduler to hide and the NaN class survives without a scalar test.

The dtype boundary is exactly two casts. The load widens BF16 with `RoundMode.NONE` and the store narrows with `RoundMode.TO_EVEN`; everything between is the same FP32 body as the `hif8_fp32` sibling. That is what makes the exact comparison legitimate: the HiFloat8 grid is a power-of-two step times a small integer, which BF16 holds without rounding.

`build_kernel(device)` binds one undecorated body to either the A2 or the A3 facade by importing `ascriptor.a2` or `ascriptor.a3` and applying `kernel(mode="vec")` at call time. The source is written once; the device is a host-side argument, and main.py's `DEVICE` is the only place it is chosen.
do_not_copy_when: You need NaN payload propagation. The non-finite path rebuilds its answer from masks and adds, so the NaN class comes back but its payload bits do not; the contract excludes payload identity for exactly that reason.

Your tile body can fault or reduce. `_quantize_tile` always runs all 512 lanes and the tail publishes only `valid` of them, which costs no branch precisely because the body is elementwise and its divisor is clamped to 2^-22 by `vmaxs` — stale lanes can hold anything. A reduction across the tile, or a divisor that can reach zero, breaks that bargain.

You want an FP8 E4M3 or E5M2 converter. HiFloat8 spends its bits differently: the mantissa narrows from 3 to 0 bits as |e| crosses 3, 7 and 15, so neither the thresholds nor the single overflow bound of 40960 transfer to a fixed-field format.

entries.title: FP32 HiFloat8 quantize-dequantize
entries.formula: y = sign(x) * round_half_away(|x| / s) * s with s = 2^(e - m), e = floor(log2|x|), m = 3/2/1/0 as |e| <= 3/7/15/above; |x| >= 40960 -> +-inf, |x| < 2^-23 -> +0; contiguous FP32 [1, total] in and out
study_for: How to derive a power-of-two scale from the exponent field instead of calling a log. `_quantize_tile` reinterprets the FP32 tile as uint16 pairs, masks with `FP32_EXP_MASK` to isolate 2^e, then gets 2^|e| by complementing the field and adding `EXP_ABS_BIAS` before a `vmax` against the original — a two-instruction reflection about the exponent bias that replaces an absolute value on the exponent itself.

A fully branch-free special-value policy. Finite, overflow and non-finite are three uint8 masks built by `compare_scalar`; the published result is the sum of three `select`ed terms, so the quantized value, the restored signed infinity and the restored NaN never contend for a lane and no lane takes a different path. The rounding is `add(+-0.5)` then a TRUNC cast, which is half-away-from-zero written with the two ops the vector unit actually has.

The tail is a slice, not a branch: `valid = Min(TILE, total - offset)` narrows only the two DMAs, while `_quantize_tile` always computes all 512 lanes. The stale lanes past `valid` are computed and discarded, which is exactly why the divisor is clamped with `vmaxs(scale, HIF8_DML_SCALE)` — no lane, live or stale, can divide by zero.

`build_kernel(device)` binds one undecorated body to either the A2 or the A3 facade by importing `ascriptor.a2` or `ascriptor.a3` and applying `kernel(mode="vec")` at call time. The source is written once; the device is a host-side argument, and main.py's `DEVICE` is the only place it is chosen.
do_not_copy_when: You need NaN payload propagation. The non-finite path rebuilds its answer from masks and adds, so the NaN class comes back but its payload bits do not; the contract excludes payload identity for exactly that reason.

Your tile body can fault or reduce. Computing the whole tile and publishing only `valid` of it is free here because the body is elementwise with a clamped divisor. A reduction across the tile, or an operation that can trap on the stale lanes, needs the mask the source deliberately does without.

You want an FP8 E4M3 or E5M2 converter. HiFloat8 narrows the mantissa from 3 bits to 0 as |e| crosses 3, 7 and 15, so neither the thresholds nor the single 40960 overflow bound transfer to a fixed-field format. Read `grouped_fp32` for the per-group E8M0/E2M1 family instead.

entries.title: MSD radix top-k on one vector core
entries.formula: values = the k largest of keys[0:count], FP32, from a fixed [1, 4096] buffer padded with -inf; indices are the input positions they came from
study_for: How a library composite is used from a kernel. The whole algorithm is one `radix_topk(cand, cidx, keys_ub, count, k)` call inside `auto_sync()`; the four most-significant-byte levels, the accumulated histogram windows and the greater/equal rank-and-scatter compaction are maintained in library, and this folder owns the launch, the inputs and the independent check. Read it to see how much a kernel can be while staying twenty lines long.

The result is a multiset, not a sequence. Raw output order is unspecified and a tied threshold makes several index sets equally correct, so `main.py` sorts the kernel's k values and compares that against `torch.topk`. Comparing the indices instead would fail a correct kernel that broke a tie differently -- `all_equal_257_33` has 257 keys at the threshold and C(257, 33) legal answers.

Signed zero is the sharp edge of the sign fold. Descending FP32 order is not the ascending order of the raw 32-bit words, so the MSD levels have to fold the sign bit; -0.0 and +0.0 then become numerically tied but still distinct words. `signed_zero_257_33` is there so a kernel that ranks raw words is caught, and it is also why the comparison cannot be on bit patterns at fixed positions.

The fixed-size buffers are part of the contract, not slack. Inputs are always DMA'd as [1, 4096] with -inf padding beyond `count`, and the outputs are always 512 slots of which only the first k are defined. The undefined suffix is what lets the DMA be a single constant-shape move with no tail branch.
do_not_copy_when: You need more than one vector core. The histogram windows, the running prefix and the remaining count live in this core's vector registers; a second core would need a cross-core reduction at every one of the four levels.
Your count exceeds 4096 or your k exceeds 512. Both are the allocation, not a parameter: `keys_ub` is [1, 4096] of UB and the candidate pair is [1, 512] each.
Your keys can be NaN or +inf. -inf is reserved here as the padding value, and a NaN has no position in the radix order at all -- the domain requires the first `count` keys to be finite.

You need the results in order, or you need the indices to be reproducible. Neither is promised: compaction publishes every strictly greater key first and then enough threshold ties to reach k, in whatever order the scatter lands them.

entries.title: Chunked row prefix scan, two storage branches
entries.formula: prefixes[r] = x[r] + prefixes[r-1] within each chunk_size row block, prefixes[chunk start] = x[chunk start], FP32 [M, H]
study_for: A serial recurrence inside a `@vf` body. `chunk_row_cumsum_vf` reads the previous row back out of the destination buffer rather than keeping it in a register across the loop, and `vf_barrier(VfPipe.STORE, VfPipe.LOAD)` after every row is what makes that store visible to the next load. Delete the barrier and the kernel still emits, still runs, and returns stale rows.

Why both storage branches are written out even though only one runs. A backend prints both arms and specialises each against the launch's actual H, so with H = 128 the unclamped narrow arm asks for a 512-byte burst into a 256-byte row with a pad stride of -8. `Min(H, VEC_WIDTH)` states what the `if H < VEC_WIDTH` guard already guarantees and costs nothing at run time; the dead arm's geometry has to be valid, not just unreached.

Host-side partitioning with `GetVecNum()`/`GetVecIdx()`: chunks are handed to vector owners in contiguous runs, so every owner's first output row starts on a 32-byte GM block. `reference.domain` rejects the M/H/chunk_size combinations where that boundary would land mid-block, which is a launch constraint, not a numerical one.

The `fp32_cancellation` case is the tolerance's justification: 1e8 + 1 rounds back to 1e8 in FP32, so the third prefix is exactly 0.0. A kernel that accumulated in FP64 or reassociated the chain would return 1.0 and be more accurate and wrong.
do_not_copy_when: You want a parallel scan. This is a strictly sequential row recurrence with one register of carry; the chunk boundary is the only place parallelism exists, and a Hillis-Steele or Blelloch scan would change the FP32 rounding order the comparison pins down.
Your H is between 64 and 128 and not a multiple of 64. The wide branch uses the GM row pitch directly and has no column tail; only H < 64 gets the padded 64-column path.

Your chunk does not fit UB. All four buffers are allocated whichever branch runs, so the budget is 2 * align32(chunk_size * H * 4) + 2 * chunk_size * 256 bytes against 256 KiB, not the size of the live branch alone.

entries.title: Integrated convolution: four stages inside one MIX launch
entries.formula: y = conv2d(x, w) with pad 2, stride 2, dilation 2; x NCHW [1,64,32,32] FP16, w OIHW [128,64,3,3] FP16, FP32 L0C accumulation, one nearest-even cast to FP16, delivered flattened as [128, 256]
study_for: This is the integrated level of a four-unit family that teaches one convolution at four depths. `native` is the cube body alone, fed image and weights the host has already packed. `layout` is the first stage alone, NCHW to NC1HWC0, with its two padding protocols. `stepwise` runs all four stages as four separate launches the host composes. This unit fuses those same four stages into a single MIX launch. Read them in that order; the arithmetic never changes, only who owns the staging.

The whole point is the barrier protocol, and it is four distinct mechanisms on four flags. `allvec_ready(F_VIN)`/`allvec_wait(F_VIN)` joins the two vector cores to each other once both the 5HD image and the fractal weights are in workspace. `vec_ready(F_VC)`/`wait_vec(F_VC)` hands that off to the cube. `allcube_ready(F_CUBE)`/`allcube_wait(F_CUBE)` joins the cube cores, and `cube_ready(F_CV)`/`wait_cube(F_CV)` releases the second vector phase. Drop any one of them and the kernel still emits; it just reads a workspace the producer has not finished writing.

`split_workspace` is what makes one launch possible: `data5hd_ws`, `wz_ws` and `nz_ws` are GM buffers the kernel allocates for itself, so the intermediates never become host tensors. The price is that nothing between the image and the final output is observable. That is why this demo has no `--stages` and `stepwise` does -- and why, when the answer is wrong, you debug it over there and port the fix back.

`X_CHUNK = 512  # halved: DBuff slots of all 3 stages share UB`. All three vector phases live in one kernel, so their double buffers are resident at the same time and each one gets half the tile it would have had on its own. That comment is the concrete cost of integration, and it is the first constant to re-derive if you change the geometry.
do_not_copy_when: You need to know which of the four stages is wrong. This launch publishes only its final [128, 256] output; a bad 5HD pad row and a bad final cast look identical from here. Use the `stepwise` sibling, which checks each stage against its own reference before composing them.

Your valuation is not B1 / Cin64 / Cout128 / 32x32 / 3x3 / pad2 / stride2 / dilation2. M = 256, K = 576, TILE_K = 96, X_CHUNK, O_CHUNK and the L1 feature-map extent are all elaborated from those numbers as literals. `DEBUG = True` names the historical 256x256 valuation, which has no corrected typed signature here.

You want more than one block. `kernel_for` pins `mode="mix", block_dim=1` because the cross-core flags coordinate cores inside one MIX group; a second block gets its own flag space and would read this one's workspace without ever waiting for it.

entries.title: NCHW to NC1HWC0, two channel-padding protocols
entries.formula: y[b, c//16, hw, c%16] = x[b, c, hw] for c < C, zero for C <= c < C1*16; FP16 [B, C, HW] -> FP16 [B*C1*HW, 16] with C1 = ceil(C/16) and HW rounded to 16 on chip only
study_for: This is the layout level of a four-unit family that teaches one convolution at four depths: `native` is the cube body alone on pre-packed inputs, this unit is the first staging stage alone, `stepwise` runs all four stages as separate launches, and `integrated` fuses them into one MIX launch. Start here -- it is the only one of the four with no arithmetic in it at all, so a wrong answer can only be a wrong address.

Two bodies, one job, and the difference is a pipe hazard. `transdata_nchw_to_5hd_half` is given a grid the host already padded to C1*16 channels, so it loads 16 full bursts and never writes src_buf from two pipes. `transdata_nchw_to_5hd_half_dup` is given only the C real channels and clears the tail itself with `dup`, which puts a V-pipe write and an MTE2-pipe load on the same buffer; `t5_dup_ready` (V->MTE2) and `t5_load_valid` (MTE2->V, preset) are the ready/valid pair that orders them. The preset on the second one is what lets the first iteration proceed.

Channel padding and spatial padding are handled in opposite directions and it is worth reading them side by side. Channels are padded up (to C1*16) and the padding is kept in the output as defined zeros. HW is padded up to 16 for the load and transpose, then `store = Min(hw - s, CHUNK)` drops those rows so the output holds exactly HW rows per plane. `*_channel_spatial_tail` is the case where both are non-trivial at once.

`NLANES = 2` with `if blk % NLANES == vec_idx` is a static owner test over (b, c1) blocks, not a computed range. When there is only one block -- the `*_idle_owner` cases -- vector 1 matches nothing, executes no store, and must still leave `auto_sync()` cleanly. The launch is `mode="mix", block_dim=1` even though no cube work exists, because one MIX group is what supplies the two vector owners the source partition assumes.
do_not_copy_when: Your shape exceeds the static GM signatures. The two input capacities are literal in the typed ABI -- 3072 elements for host_pad, 1920 for ub_pad -- and the output is [144, 16]; `geometry` in reference.py refuses anything larger rather than letting it overflow. B2/C20/HW36 is exactly at both input limits.

You want the convolution itself. Nothing here multiplies or accumulates; this stage only moves halves into the layout the cube expects. Read `native` for the cube body, or `stepwise` for this stage followed by the other three.

You are tempted to copy the `dup` from the ub_pad body without its two SEvents. The whole reason the host_pad variant exists is that pre-zeroing a UB buffer from the V pipe races the MTE2 load into the same buffer; the handshake is not boilerplate around the dup, it is the reason the dup is legal.

entries.title: Native convolution, four cube bodies
entries.formula: out[b, cout, ho, wo] = bias[cout] + sum over c, kh, kw of x[b, c, ho*s + kh*d - pad, wo*s + kw*d - pad] * w[cout, c, kh, kw]; FP16 NC1HWC0 image and Cout/C1/Kh/Kw/C0 weights in, FP32 NZ [B*((COUT+15)//16)*M_PAD, 16] out
study_for: This is the native level of a four-unit family that teaches one convolution at four depths: `layout` is the NCHW-to-NC1HWC0 staging stage alone, `stepwise` runs the staging and this cube as four host-composed launches, `integrated` fuses them into one MIX launch. Native is the cube by itself -- reference.py's `pack` hands it NC1HWC0 planes and Cout/C1/Kh/Kw/C0 weights already built, so nothing in kernel.py transposes anything. Read it first if what you want is the convolution and not the plumbing.

The M padding is computed, not junk, and that is why `physical_nz` is a checked output beside `output`. `M_PAD` is the physical output plane (64, 48 or 224) and the M loop runs over all of it, so when HO*WO is smaller the window keeps sliding past the last real row and produces real values (D-223). The reference reproduces them by extending the FP64 image with `extra_rows * stride` of bottom zeros -- independently of the device's load3d addressing. Checking only the logical NCHW crop would leave a third of some cases unchecked.

Every body allocates L1 and L0C at its mode's static worst case and masks the tail with runtime scalars: `fm <<= data[:, :]` stages the full capacity, and `h`, `w`, `c`, `cout`, `m_pad` tell `conv2d` what is real inside it. The `C_MAX`/`H_MAX`/`W_MAX`/`COUT_MAX` quadruples are chosen pairwise distinct from every GM dimension so OpExec's scalar-to-dimension auto-match stays unambiguous -- change one and a scalar can silently bind to the wrong axis.

`geometry` in reference.py refuses a valuation the hardware cannot serve, and the rule that matters is `ceil(M_PAD / TILE_M) * TILE_M > align16(HO*WO)`. That is the historical A5 large 14x14 with M_PAD 224 defect (RFC-0011 s7.31): align16(196) is 208, the M loop runs to 224, and the last tiles leave the output plane. 14x16 and 16x14 both give 224 valid positions and are the valuations this demo keeps.

Four bodies, one shape of code. `basic` is the plain FP16 accumulation; `bias` adds a BT bias that `conv2d` applies on the first K tile only, which `bias_two_k_tiles` pins down with a zero image and a K that spans two tiles; `dilation` combines stride 2 with dilation 2; `large` keeps a 4x4 filter resident in L1 with `PAD = (1, 2, 1, 2)` -- an even filter cannot be padded symmetrically -- and reloads the feature map once per batch.
do_not_copy_when: You are targeting the pypto backend. `conv2d` desugars into `dma.l1_to_l0.img2col` for the A operand of every mmad, and that opcode is outside the pypto surface (upstream gap A5-UP-005); see the comment at the top of main.py. cce and pto_isa run every case.

You need more than one cube core. Every `kernel_for_*` binds `block_dim=1`. `large` still carries its source `MULTICORE` gate around the M loop, but with `MULTICORE = 1` it is a no-op; a real multi-core valuation for these bodies is not declared here.

Your shape is outside the mode's static capacity. The four capacity quadruples -- (32, 8, 8, 48) for basic and bias, (16, 12, 12, 32) for dilation, (32, 16, 16, 64) for large -- are baked into the L1 extents and the typed GM signatures, and `large` additionally requires exactly COUT 64 and two batches.

You want the image already in NCHW. This kernel reads NC1HWC0 and a fractal weight layout only; the packing lives in reference.py here, and in a real pipeline it is a separate kernel -- read the `layout` and `stepwise` siblings for that half.

entries.title: Stepwise convolution: four kernels the host composes
entries.formula: y = conv2d(x, w) with pad 2, stride 2, dilation 2; x NCHW [1,64,32,32] FP16, w OIHW [128,64,3,3] FP16, staged as 5HD [4608,16] FP16, fractal [128,576] FP16, NZ [2048,16] FP32, then NCHW [128,256] FP16
study_for: This is the stepwise level of a four-unit family that teaches one convolution at four depths. `native` is the cube body alone on pre-packed inputs; `layout` is the first staging stage alone with its two padding protocols; this unit runs all four stages as four host-composed launches; `integrated` fuses the same four into one MIX launch with cross-core flags. Stepwise is the one to debug in: its intermediates are ordinary host tensors, so every stage boundary is inspectable.

`--stages` is a different question from the default run, not a louder version of it. The default chains the four kernels on each other's real output. `--stages` feeds each kernel an input reference.py built by hand -- stage 3 gets hand-packed 5HD and hand-packed fractal weights, stage 4 gets a tensor of FP16 midpoint probes instead of the cube's output -- so a failure is that stage's own defect rather than an inherited one. Run both: one finds a broken stage, the other finds a broken hand-off.

Tolerance is per output, and three of the four stages have none. `data5hd`, `weights_fractal` and `cast_nchw` are bitwise, because two of them only move halves to new addresses and the third is one specified rounding -- `RoundMode.TO_EVEN`, checked against the host's own `struct.pack('<e')`. Only `conv_nz` and the final `output` round anything. Writing that as one tolerance for the whole unit would have thrown away three exact claims.

Each stage owns its width. `kernel_for_x_to_5hd`, `kernel_for_w_to_fractal` and `kernel_for_out_to_nchw` bind `mode="vec", block_dim=2`; `kernel_for_conv_compute` binds `mode="cube", block_dim=1`. The three vector stages partition statically with `per_lane = (units + N_VEC - 1) // N_VEC` against `N_VEC = 2`, so a one-core launch would silently never execute lane 1's half of the units -- the case's `block_dim: 1` describes the pipeline's launch group, not any one kernel's width.
do_not_copy_when: You want the fused version. Four launches mean four GM round trips for tensors that never had to leave the chip; `integrated` keeps all three intermediates in `split_workspace` and pays for it with buffers that no longer fit full-size (its X_CHUNK is halved). Read both before choosing.

Your valuation is not B1 / Cin64 / Cout128 / 32x32 / 3x3 / pad2 / stride2 / dilation2. `common.py` elaborates M = 256, K = 576, HP = H + 4, TILE_K = 96 and both chunk sizes from those numbers as literals, and every stage's typed GM signature is derived from them. `DEBUG = True` names the historical 256x256 valuation, which has no corrected typed signature here.

Your convolution needs runtime top/bottom padding. The two pad rows above and below each plane are baked into the 5HD tensor as zero rows by stage 1, which is why the `Conv2D` descriptor pads left/right only and the cube can take a fixed five-row feature-map slice per output row with no boundary branch.

entries.title: Gated activations: five GELU modes and three SwiGLU precisions
entries.formula: gelu_tanh: y = x / (1 + exp(-2*sqrt(2/pi) * (x + 0.044715*x^3))); gelu_erf: y = (x/2 + |z|/sqrt(2)) - tail_AS7.1.26(|z|), z = x/sqrt(2); swiglu: y = (x0*x1) / (1 + exp(-beta*x0)) with x split on its last dimension; FP32 arithmetic throughout, FP32 / FP16 / BF16 storage
study_for: Eight complete activations in one folder, so the axis that changes is visible. Every mode computes in FP32 and differs only in its storage dtype, its UB tile capacity and, for GELU, which approximation it uses. `make_kernel(variant, device)` picks one; the narrow modes add exactly two casts, a `RoundMode.NONE` widen on the way in (exact, so no rounding decision) and an explicit `RoundMode.TO_EVEN` narrow on the way out. Reading gelu_tanh_f32 beside gelu_tanh_bf16 shows precisely what supporting a narrow dtype costs.

The erf body's final subtraction is not simplified, on purpose. `(x*0.5 + halfabs) - tail` cancels for negative x, and rewriting it algebraically -- which is correct in exact arithmetic -- changes the answer in FP32 exactly where GELU is smallest. The `mode_band` cases feed x = -2.5 for that reason, and they are also what separates the tanh answer from the erf answer, which agree almost everywhere else.

The SwiGLU split is an ABI, not a reshape. The last dimension is cropped to an even width first, then each contiguous half is flattened into its own operand; flattening the whole tensor and splitting the result afterwards is a different operation on any rank above 1 or any odd width, which is what `split_order` and `source_odd` pin down. The host also passes -beta as a scalar narrowed to FP32, because the kernel's denominator is exp(-beta*x0) + 1 and forming it on the device would add a rounding the reference does not have.

The tiling is the same in all eight: `valid = Min(tile_len, n - n0)` with `[0:1, 0:valid]` windows on every load, compute and store, and cores taking contiguous runs of whole tiles from `GetVecNum()`/`GetVecIdx()`. `single_value` (one element, one-element tile) and `two_cores_tail` (a final tile of one) are the cheapest cases that break a kernel which computes a full tile and stores a windowed one.
do_not_copy_when: You are on A5. This is the A2/A3 tensor-vector vocabulary -- `mul`, `muls`, `exp`, `div` over UB tiles -- not the A5 `@vf` register surface. Read examples/axpy for that.

You want GELU by the erf polynomial at FP16. There is no such body here: the original float16 `approximate='none'` caller selected the tanh body and then compared it against an erf reference, and that inconsistent selector was retired rather than given a kernel.

Your tile is larger than the mode allows. 6656 for tanh, 5120 for erf, 8192 for FP32 SwiGLU and 6144 for narrow SwiGLU are the UB allocations compiled into each body, not runtime parameters -- and the erf body's larger temporary set is why its number is the smallest.

Your SwiGLU beta is outside [0, 2], or your GELU input outside [-10, 10]. Both are the domain these tolerances were measured against; beyond them `exp` saturates and the elementwise bounds stop meaning anything.

entries.title: MurmurHash3 fmix32 finalizer on INT32 carriers
entries.formula: h = x mod 2^32; h ^= h >> 16; h = h * 0x85EBCA6B mod 2^32; h ^= h >> 13; h = h * 0xC2B2AE35 mod 2^32; h ^= h >> 16; int32 tensor in, int32 tensor out, same shape, up to 1048576 values in tiles of at most 8192
study_for: Three reinterprets and no dtype conversion. The INT32 tensor is the carrier; `h_i32.reinterpret(DT.uint32)` is what makes `shiftrs` a logical shift instead of an arithmetic one that would copy the sign bit into the top 16 bits, and `reinterpret(DT.uint16)` gives the halves that `vor`/`vand`/`vnot` compose into a 32-bit XOR. Nothing is converted, only re-viewed, so the payload bits never pass through a numeric domain that could round them.

`_mul_const` calls `dup` to materialize the full 32-bit constant into an INT32 tensor before `mul`. That is deliberate: a scalar multiply-by-immediate takes a float path whose mantissa cannot hold a 32-bit odd constant times a 32-bit payload, and the low bits — the only bits a hash mixer cares about — come out wrong. The constants are pre-converted by `_as_int32`, because 0x85EBCA6B and 0xC2B2AE35 are both above 2^31.

The partition is read at run time, not baked in. `GetVecNum()` and `GetVecIdx()` with `CeilDiv` give each owner a contiguous run of tiles, so one body serves block_dim 1 and block_dim 2 with no host branch; `valid = Min(tile_len, n - n0)` and the `[0:1, 0:valid]` windows on the load, the five stages and the store are the entire tail handling. `two_cores_tail` is the case where both meet: six tiles over two owners with a final tile of five values.

`h_ub` is a `DBuff` indexed by `h_ub[tile_idx]`, which selects a slot modulo 2 so the next tile's load can overlap the current tile's compute under `auto_sync()`. `source_7` (8256 values, two tiles on one owner) is the smallest case that actually reuses a slot; a single-tile case never exercises the hand-off.
do_not_copy_when: You need MurmurHash3 of a message. This is the fmix32 finalizer alone — no block mixing, no length incorporation, no tail rules. Applied to data it is a bit mixer, not a hash of that data.

You want a random-number generator with statistical or cryptographic properties. The counter case shows the map is a permutation of 32-bit values and nothing more; there is no independence claim here, and it is not Philox.

Your tile exceeds 8192 values, or your owners do not start on a 32-byte GM boundary. The three UB tensors are [1, 8192] INT32 and the DBuff doubles the first one; the boundary rule is `per_core * tile_len * 4 % 32 == 0`, which `geometry` in reference.py refuses rather than silently misaligning an owner.

entries.title: Blockwise E5M2 quantization of a cube product
entries.formula: product = X^T @ Y on the cube in FP32, then per 128-column row block: scale = max(abs(row)) / 224 and payload = e5m2(row / scale)
study_for: The cube-to-vector bridge is the shape to take away: the FP32 L0C tile is handed to the vector unit through a `CvMutex` whose pipes belong to the consumer, and the vector side then owns both outputs. Nothing goes back to the cube.

Two store paths for the same arithmetic, selected per case by `variant`. `default` writes the normalized `RegList` into an E5M2 UB tile and lets the store convert; `pack4` casts each half explicitly with a ZERO-layout `CastConfig` and stores two PACK4 halves. Comparing them is the point — they must produce identical bytes.

Why the payload is compared bit for bit and the scale is not. The payload is the published ABI: a consumer reads those bytes back, and the E5M2 grid plus the nearest-even tie rule fixes every one of them, so there is nothing a tolerance could be about. The scale is arithmetic — an FP32 row maximum over 224 — so it gets a tight allowance and a relative residual that stops a vacuous scale from passing on atol.

`pack4_reuse` is skipped under the simulator, with the reason printed, and this is the most instructive thing in the folder. The functional simulator computes a host FP32 matrix product; silicon uses the cube's own reduction tree, which the source does not specify. At row 376, column 113 the two land on either side of an E5M2 midpoint — neighbours 20 and 24, midpoint 22 — so the model normalizes to 22.000002 and encodes 78 while silicon normalizes to 21.999983 and encodes 77. The independent reference agrees with silicon. Run that case under `--launcher aclnn` or `board`. The tolerance is deliberately not widened: a host accumulation order does not become a hardware oracle by making a simulation pass.
The midpoint cases exist for that same reason at a smaller scale: `default_midpoints` and `pack4_midpoints` put the normalized values exactly on the ties, where the rounding rule is the whole answer.
do_not_copy_when: Your quantization block is not a 128-column row block. The 224 divisor, the row maximum and the E5M2 range are one design; changing the block changes all three.

You want a general fp8 cast example. This one is about getting eight-bit values out of a vector register two different ways and proving they agree — read online_mx for the MX formats and their shared-scale layout.
You need the simulator to be the oracle. One case here is a located disagreement between the simulator and silicon, and no amount of kernel work closes it.

entries.title: Matrix product, four row normalizations
entries.formula: out[M, N] = (X[M, K] @ Y[N, K].T) / d, where d is the row sum, the row L2 norm, or the per-128-column absmax; FP16 in, FP32 out
study_for: One pass or two, decided by where the denominator's input lives. `row_sum_small` fits a whole N=256 row in one L0C tile, so the reduction and the division happen in the same vector call. `row_sum_large` cannot: the row sum is not known until every N tile has been produced, so pass 1 accumulates it into a persistent UB tensor and parks the raw product in the output tensor, `bar_all()` separates the passes, and pass 2 reloads and divides. Read the two side by side before choosing a shape for your own reduction.

The output tensor doubles as the pipeline's scratch. In the two-pass variants pass 1 writes un-normalized products into the caller's `z`/`out` and pass 2 overwrites them in place, which is why `reloadbuf`/`reload_ub` exists as a third UB buffer: reloading into the pass-1 buffer would alias the next tile's cube-owned FIX publication.

`row_sum_large_first_k_tail` is a kept bug. At K=130 the second K tile fills only 2 of its slot's 128 rows, and a matmul that contracts the whole slot reads a never-written buffer's poison, where 0 * NaN is NaN -- all 16384 outputs came back NaN. The fix is the explicit `k=valid_k` on the `matmul`, and the comment above it in kernel.py records why K=260 hid the defect: two full tiles fill both slots before the tail arrives.

`block_absmax_single` (M=1) and `block_absmax_tail` (M=65) exercise the `if rows > 0` guard. The 128-row bridge is split into two fixed 64-row vector halves, so a small M leaves the second half owning one row or none; without the guard the idle peer would construct `z[64:64]` beyond the tensor. Its `cvmutex` handshakes stay outside the guard, because a vector peer that owns no rows must still take part in the synchronization.
do_not_copy_when: Your denominator can reach zero. There is no epsilon anywhere: the row-sum variants only work because their inputs are generated strictly positive, and a signed input would let the sum cancel through zero and divide by it.

Your shape does not meet the variant's alignment. `row_sum_small` is fixed at N=256, K=128 and M%128; `row_sum_large` and `row_l2` need M%64 and N%256 and take any K; `block_absmax` needs N%128. These are the source's own guards, and nothing in the kernels re-checks them. `row_l2` is the one place this folder inherited a guard the port does not have: its K loop bounds every operand with `valid_k = Min(TILE_K, K - k0)` exactly as `row_sum_large` does, and `row_l2_k_unaligned` runs K=130 to hold that open.

You want a fused epilogue after a matmul in general. The one-pass variants are only possible because the denominator is local to the data already on chip; the moment it is not, you are writing the two-pass form and paying a full re-read of the product.

entries.title: Online MX quantization and MX matrix product
entries.formula: output = dequant(E4M3 payload, E8M0 scale per 32 K values)(x) @ dequant(...)(y)^T, FP32 in and out, K = 64 as two groups of 32
study_for: One recipe in two physical layouts. `nd` reads [16, 64] with rows as the logical rows and writes payload bytes straight through; `transposed` reads [64, 32] with columns as the logical rows, and its VF interleaves neighbouring row bytes and scatters UINT16 pairs. That pair scatter is the format, not an optimization -- replacing it with a plain byte scatter produces a payload the cube reads in the wrong order.

The single-publisher discipline around `VcMutex`. Both vector sub-blocks compute identical tiles but only sub 0 stores them into L1, so the L1 writes have exactly one writer. `vcmutex.ready()` deliberately stays outside that `if GetSubBlockIdx() == 0`: the cube waits for both sub-blocks' ready, and sub 1's fires on an empty MTE3 queue. Move the ready inside the guard and the launch deadlocks.

E8M0 byte 0 means 2^-127 here, and that is a property of the consumer, not of the format. The VF clamps the FP32 normalization to 2^-127 when the biased exponent bits are zero, which is what this MX matmul also assumes; a separate E8M0-to-BF16 conversion instruction maps byte 0 to zero instead. `nd_scale_byte_zero` and `transposed_scale_byte_zero` exist to pin which of the two rules this code follows.

How to make an internal boundary comparable. The composition keeps payload and scales in L1 where nothing can read them, so `kernel.py` also carries two leaf kernels that run the very same VFs on one vector owner and publish those bytes to GM. `main.py --stages` compares them bitwise against an independent IEEE encoder, which turns 'the product is slightly off' into 'this exponent byte is wrong'. The destinations start at byte 255, which is not a legal scale, so an unwritten byte is visible.
do_not_copy_when: Your K is not 64. The recipe is exactly two 32-element groups per logical row, and both the scale staging (one masked 128-byte tile) and the packed 32/64-byte scale row are sized for that.
Your inputs can be NaN or infinite. There is no finite scale for an all-255 exponent, and the E4M3 encoder here is finite-only: code 127 is rejected rather than treated as NaN.

You need more than one work item per launch. The kernel factories accept a batched ABI, but the shipped entries are the source's one-item partition, which puts all the work on cube group 0 -- any extra MIX group requested stays idle, which is what `nd_idle_groups` shows.

You want to reuse the scale path for a different MX consumer. Both the byte-0 meaning and the [row, group] byte order are agreed with this `matmul_mx` call; a consumer with either convention changed needs a different publication, not a different reader.

entries.title: SIMT transpose of a cube product, two index orders
entries.formula: out[N, M] = (A[M, K] @ B[N, K].T).T, FP32 throughout, whole matrices at M,N <= 64 and K <= 64
study_for: What `@simt` is, against `@vf`. A vector function is written once and applies to a whole register; a SIMT body is written from one thread's point of view and the launch runs 1024 of them, so the loop is `for i in range(simt_thread_id(), total, simt_thread_num())` and every question about correctness becomes a question about which thread owns which element. This is the smallest complete example of that surface.

One transpose, two legitimate index decompositions, and only one destination can be contiguous. `contiguous_read` takes `row = i // N, col = i % N`, so `i` walks the UB tile in order and the GM write is strided by M; `contiguous_write` takes `col = i // M, row = i % M` and gets the opposite trade. The two kernels are otherwise identical, so the pair isolates exactly that choice. This unit ranks neither.

Why only sub-block 0 publishes. The cube result is copied to both vector peers -- `l0c_to_ub` twice with `sub_block_id=0` then `1` -- under one `CvMutex`, but the SIMT body runs under `if GetSubBlockIdx() == 0`. The original source let both peers write the same GM elements and the values agreed, which is exactly why it looked safe: two non-atomic writers of one element is a write-write hazard regardless of what they write.

The thread population is fixed at 1024 while the work is not, and the cases span both sides of it. `thread_tail` (256 elements) leaves three quarters of the threads never entering the loop; `loop_reuse` (3072 elements) makes every thread take three strided visits. Those are different failure modes -- an inactive thread that writes anyway, and a stride that revisits or skips -- and a single shape tests neither.
do_not_copy_when: Your matrices do not fit on chip whole. L1, L0C and UB here each hold the entire matrix, which is what lets the SIMT body index a flat tile with no tiling at all; the bound is M,N <= 64 and K <= 64, and past it this structure has no answer.

You want more than one core or more than one vector peer working. Cube group 0 owns the whole operation and sub-block 0 alone publishes; `block_dim` above 1 only adds idle groups, and that is deliberate, not an oversight to fix.
The values your threads write are all equal and you are tempted to let two of them write. That is the exact mistake this unit was corrected for -- agreement between writers is not ownership.

entries.title: Symmetric 2x2 covariance inverse
entries.formula: det = f32(f32(c00*c11) - f32(c01*c01)); inv00 = c11/det, inv01 = -(c01/det), inv11 = c00/det, over three FP32 [N] tensors
study_for: Three tensors in, three out, because a symmetric 2x2 has three distinct values. Storing c10 as well would let a caller hand in a matrix that disagrees with itself, so the public ABI is c00, c01, c11 and main.py's `execute` bridges them to the kernel's [N, 1] with a shape-only reshape. The kernel never sees a 2x2.

What a closed form without a fallback looks like. `det` is formed once from two products and one subtraction and then divided by three times, with no epsilon, no regularization and no singular branch. A matrix outside the declared domain produces an infinity, which is visible, instead of a smoothed answer that is not the inverse of anything.

`small_offdiagonal` is the case that justifies the residual bound. With c01 = 2^-16 the true inv01 is far below atol=1e-4, so a kernel that writes zeros there passes `torch.allclose` on its own merits; only the relative L2 residual notices the output carries no signal. Copy the pair, not just the tolerance.

A UB row of one useful float. The GM tensors are [N, 1], the UB tiles are [CHUNK, 8], and the six `DBuff`s load 1 real column into an 8-wide row, compute in scalar `Reg`s, and slice the padding off again on the way out. It is the cheapest possible demonstration of why a UB pitch and a GM pitch are different numbers.
do_not_copy_when: Your matrices can be singular or near-singular. The domain here is |entries| <= 16, |det| >= 2^-10 and condition number <= 64, and nothing in the kernel checks it; a determinant that reaches zero divides by zero.

Your matrix is larger than 2x2, or not symmetric. This is an algebraic closed form written out by hand, not a factorization: 3x3 doubles the expression count and a general inverse needs pivoting, which this structure has nowhere to put.
You need every lane of the vector unit busy. One scalar `Reg` per matrix entry is what makes the formula readable at this size and is exactly what wastes the machine at a larger one.

entries.title: Quaternion to rotation, channel layout
entries.formula: rotation[9, N] = row-major 3x3 matrix of each normalized quaternion column (w, x, y, z) of q[4, N], FP32 throughout
study_for: The channel layout is the whole design. `[4, N]` in and `[9, N]` out means each quaternion component and each rotation channel is one contiguous GM row, so all thirteen transfers are whole-row DMA and the kernel needs no gather and no stride arithmetic. The caller pays for it with an explicit transpose; `quaternion_rows` is the same maths under the opposite trade.

`source_90` is the reason the variant exists. A GM row is written in 32-byte blocks, so when N is not a multiple of 8 two vector writers of neighbouring tiles touch the same physical block: the original MIX launch produced twelve real GM write-write hazards on N=90 while returning numerically identical results. `single_vector_unaligned` runs the identical body with exactly one vector owner. Numerical equality does not excuse a hazard, and the fix is ownership, not a barrier.

One tail path, expressed as a slice. `valid = Min(TILE, N - col0)` narrows every load and every store, so N=1 and N=17 write exactly their own columns and the remainder of the 64-wide UB row is never published. There is no second code path for the tail to drift from.

Nine outputs, three scratch buffers. `ub_a`, `ub_b` and `ub_norm` are reused across all nine channel formulas, which is why the body is a long straight line: each channel is computed, stored to its own `ub_Rxx`, and the scratch is immediately free again. `kernel_for(device, mode)` builds the same body for a2 or a3 and for the mix or single-vector launch.
do_not_copy_when: Your N is not a multiple of 8 and you want more than one vector writer. The 32-byte GM block is physical; this unit answers an unaligned pitch by narrowing to one owner, not by adding synchronization between writers.
You want the `[N, 4]` -> `[N, 9]` row layout. That is `quaternion_rows`: a scalar `@vf` over padded UB rows (4 padded to 8, 9 padded to 16), not a re-tiling of this kernel.

Your quaternions can be zero or denormal. No epsilon is added and a zero quaternion is never silently mapped to identity: the domain requires a squared norm in [2^-20, 2^20], and outside it the in-place `div` by `ub_norm` is a division by zero.

entries.title: Quaternion to rotation, row layout
entries.formula: rotation[N, 9] = row-major 3x3 matrix of each normalized quaternion row (w, x, y, z) of q[N, 4], FP32 throughout
study_for: Padding as the price of the natural layout. A quaternion row is 4 floats and a rotation row is 9, neither of which is a usable UB pitch, so `qbuf` is [CHUNK, 8] and `Rbuf` is [CHUNK, 16]: the load brings in 4 real columns of an 8-wide row, the vector function writes 9 of 16, and the GM store slices `[0:valid_rows, 0:OUT_COLS]` to drop the rest. The padding is never published and never read.

Scalar registers, not vector ones. `quat_to_rotation_vf` loads `qbuf[i:i+1, 0:1].single()` and stores `out_r.single_value()` nine times per row, so a `Reg` here holds one lane rather than a whole vector. Read it beside `quaternion_channels`, which computes the identical formula with full-width `mul`/`add` over [4, N] channels: same maths, opposite register discipline, and the layout is what decides which one you can write.

`DBuff` plus a bare `buf_cnt` counter is the whole double buffer. `qbuf[buf_cnt]` and `Rbuf[buf_cnt]` select the slot, `buf_cnt += 1` advances it, and `auto_sync()` inserts the events that let the next chunk's load overlap this chunk's compute. `slot_reuse` (N=161, six chunks on one vector) is the case that actually cycles the slots.

The tail is one `Min`. `valid_rows = Min(CHUNK, N - row0)` narrows the load, the `for i in range(rows)` loop inside the vector function, and the store together, so N=1, N=17 and N=1025 all run the same code with no separate tail path.
do_not_copy_when: Your quaternions are already channel-major, or you can afford to transpose them. `quaternion_channels` then loads whole contiguous rows and uses full-width vector ops instead of nine scalar stores per quaternion.
Your per-row payload is large. The 4-to-8 and 9-to-16 padding is cheap because the rows are tiny; at a wide row the same pattern wastes most of the UB tile and most of the DMA.

Your quaternions can be zero or denormal. No epsilon is added and a zero quaternion is never silently mapped to identity: the domain requires a squared norm in [2^-20, 2^20], and outside it `w <<= w / norm` divides by zero.

entries.title: Weighted 32-byte block gather with two-tap half accumulation
entries.formula: blk[r][l] = src[off[8r + l/16]/2 + l%16]; out[128t + l] = half(half(w[2t]*blk[2t][l]) + half(w[2t+1]*blk[2t+1][l])), r<4, l<128, t<2; float16 [1,512] source, int32 [1,32] byte offsets, float16 [1,16] weights -> float16 [1,256]
study_for: The half <-> uint16 reinterpret around `gather_block`. c220's vgatherb takes unsigned-short operands for 16-bit data, so `gathered_u16` and `src0_u16` are reinterpret views of the same UB tensors the half arithmetic below then reads. The aliasing is the point: the gather writes bytes, the `mul` reads halves, and dropping the reinterpret costs you a hardware compile error ('1st parameter maybe need a type `__ubuf__ unsigned short *`') rather than a wrong number.

The two strides on `mul` are the whole schedule: `src1_blk_stride=0` reuses one broadcast weight across the eight 16-half blocks of its repeat, and `src1_rep_stride=1` advances one block per repeat. That is repeatMode=false spelled out. Change either and the kernel still runs and still writes 256 plausible halves — the `permuted` and `repeated` cases exist because that failure is invisible under in-order addresses.

One complete output needs one owner. `kernel_for` pins `mode="vec"` and `block_dim=1` because the source ran this body under implicit MIX, where both vector participants owned the whole 256-value output and wrote the same bytes twice. Every numeric case in this demo passes under that defect; only a pipe-level duplicate-write control catches it, which is why the launch is fixed in the kernel file instead of left to the caller.

Bitwise comparison here is a claim about the arithmetic, not a default. The kernel rounds to half after the product and again after the tap sum; `product_rounding` picks operands whose cancellation only happens if the product was rounded first, and `half_midpoint` lands on an exact half midpoint so nearest-even is distinguishable from truncation. Without those two cases the tolerance-free comparison would prove nothing.
do_not_copy_when: You want general bilinear image interpolation. This is the fixed recipe it came from: four gather repeats, eight blocks each, two horizontal taps, 256 outputs. Tap count, repeat count and a partial trailing block are not parameters — they are baked into the UB shapes and the tap slicing.

Your offsets are not aligned 32-byte block addresses inside 0..992. `gather_block` moves whole 32-byte blocks out of a 1024-byte source; an unaligned or out-of-range offset reads past the buffer instead of clamping, and nothing in the kernel checks.

You need more than one vector core, or an output wider than 256 halves. There is no partitioning at all: the tap adds slice a single UB tensor, and a second core would re-write the same output rather than take half of it.

entries.title: Dense attention backward stage, BF16 dQK and HiFloat8 gV
entries.formula: dQK = BF16(P * (dO @ V^T - rowsum(O * dO)) / sqrt(128)); gQ = dQK @ K, gK = dQK^T @ Q, gV = BF16(HiFloat8(P))^T @ dO; BF16 [B,H,S,128] in and out, FP32 accumulators, D fixed at 128
study_for: Two different precision boundaries in one kernel, and why each needs its own model. dQK is narrowed to BF16 before gQ and gK are contracted; the gV path instead stores the probabilities through HiFloat8 (`quantize_prob_chunk_nonneg_simple` in kernel.py) and only then multiplies by dO. reference.py builds both independently -- `narrow_away` encodes the sign/exponent/fraction bits of a nearest-ties-away narrowing, `value_table` enumerates every HiFloat8 code -- so the comparison never borrows the device codec it is supposed to be checking.

The two `state_mode` values are two different claims, not two seeds. `prepared` replaces O with this module's own forward output, so the saved row statistics really are a forward pass's and the gradients are that attention's gradients. `source_arbitrary` keeps a randomly drawn O: it exercises the stage ABI at a state no forward produced, and its numbers are not a derivative of anything. Read make_inputs before reusing either.

Tail subblocks that own zero rows still have to complete the vec->cube handoff (kernel.py, the comment above the SUBS_M loop): a lane that skips its notify because it had no rows leaves the cube side waiting forever. The masking helpers `zero_half_suffix_invalid` and `apply_prob_tail_mask` are the other half of the same problem -- invalid columns are zeroed rather than left as whatever the previous tile wrote.

The three gradients accumulate through `atomic_add()` into core-shared flat GM workspaces, not through per-core rings. That is why the initialization and final-cast schedule is bound to `GetCubeNum() * 2` runtime vector lanes rather than to a fixed divisor: every accumulator chunk must be owned by exactly one lane for zeroing and exactly one for the final cast.
do_not_copy_when: Your head dimension is not 128. TILE_M/TILE_N/TILE_K are all 128 and the L1/L0C budget, the HIF8_CHUNK_M=16 quantization chunk and the half-tile UB staging were sized against that single number.
You want a causal or masked backward. This stage is dense: every query row sees every key, and the only masking is tail masking of rows and columns that do not exist.

You need gV at the same precision as gQ and gK. The HiFloat8 probability store is deliberate source behaviour and costs gV roughly an order of magnitude more relative error than the other two gradients -- it is a property of this stage, not a tolerance to be tightened.
You are on A5. This uses the A2/A3 tensor-vector vocabulary and `atomic_add()` GM accumulation; the A5 demos in this repository publish through a different surface.

entries.title: Block32-causal attention, six schedules
entries.formula: out = softmax(mask(Q @ K^T / sqrt(128))) @ V with mask key // 32 <= query // 32, top-left aligned; FP16 [BH*S, 128] Q/K/V and FP16 probabilities, FP32 out plus FP32 rowmax and rowsum
study_for: Six schedules, one algorithm, one file. v1 is a two-slot lag-1 partition, v2 adds a next-query prefetch with independent producer and consumer counters, v3 deepens the lag to three over a four-slot snake, v4 batches four key tiles into a group, v5 adds an eight-tile V preload ring, v6 flattens each core's (m_tile, group) work into one continuous stream so the pipeline fills once at the start instead of once per M tile. Every case names a variant and changes nothing else, so the six are directly comparable on the same four shapes.

The constants that are not shared are the point of merging the six into one file. All six define TILE_M/TILE_N/BLOCK_CAUSAL identically, and all six share every masking helper (`build_suffix_invalid_mask`, `apply_diagonal_tile_block32_causal_mask` and the rest) byte for byte -- so those appear once. What does not de-duplicate is v4's lookahead-two/four-slot ring against v5 and v6's lookahead-three/five-slot ring, kept apart here as `V4_GROUP_LOOKAHEAD`/`V4_GROUP_STAGE_SLOTS` versus `GROUP_LOOKAHEAD`/`GROUP_STAGE_SLOTS`. Six separate modules hid that difference behind one name.

Why every variant has a `ring_wrap` case at 769 tokens. The workspace rings are GMBuffs: the producer writes slot `g % SLOTS` while the consumer reads slot `(g - LOOKAHEAD) % SLOTS`, so the ring must be strictly larger than the lookahead or the two alias. A shape small enough to never wrap proves nothing about that invariant, and both simulators model the slot reuse and the mutex depth that enforce it.

Three outputs, and the row statistics are the diagnostic. `rowmax` and `rowsum` are the FP32 state captured before the probabilities are rounded to FP16, so main.py holds them to 1e-05 while `out` gets 0.005 -- if `out` is wrong and the statistics are right, the fault is in PV, not in the softmax. They are published per head at a stride padded to a multiple of eight FP32 values so two heads never share a 32-byte GM line, and `execute` slices that padding off on the host rather than in the kernel.
do_not_copy_when: Your causal mask is per token. This is a block staircase at BLOCK_CAUSAL = 32: every query in a 32-token block sees exactly the same key prefix, which is what lets whole diagonal tiles be masked with one helper instead of row by row.

Your head dimension is not 128, or your tiles are not 128x128. TILE_M/TILE_N/TILE_K and the half-tile vector sub-blocks are all that number, and the L1/L0C budgets of all six schedules were sized against it.

You want the simplest possible starting point. v1 is the one to read first and the other five are variations on it -- start anywhere else and you will be reading pipeline bookkeeping before you have read the algorithm.
Your S2 is below 64 and you want v5 or v6. Their disjoint V backfill reads 128 - valid_n rows from the head of the tensor, and shorter sequences do not have those rows to read.

entries.title: Forward attention, nine A2/A3 sources
entries.formula: out = softmax(mask(Q @ K^T / sqrt(D))) @ V over head-major [rows, D] tensors, D 128 or 256, FP16 or BF16 in, FP32 or BF16 out, probabilities stored in FP16, BF16 or HiFloat8; pv_stage instead publishes the unnormalized exp(score - rowmax) @ V of each 128-key tile
study_for: Nine sources that differ in ABI, not only in schedule -- and MODELS in reference.py is what lets one reference formula serve all nine. Each entry names the key-group size the online softmax rescales at, the precision the probabilities are stored in before PV, whether the mask is causal, and whether the variant publishes normalized attention or unnormalized partial PV. Read MODELS before reading any kernel body: it is the shortest statement of what each variant actually computes.

`pv_stage` is in this family and is not attention. It publishes S2 // 128 unnormalized partial PV results per query row and never divides by a denominator, which is why its comparison carries atol 2e-2 -- the numbers have not been scaled back down by a softmax denominator, so an absolute bound on them is not the same quantity as an absolute bound on an attention output. Copying its tolerance onto a normalized kernel would be a much weaker check than it looks.

Why the elementwise bounds are loose and the relative L2 is the real gate. The probabilities are stored at the source's own precision, so one that lands near a rounding midpoint of that format goes to opposite neighbours under two independent exp() implementations. A single straddle is derived to cost up to 1.5e-02 at D=256 while moving the relative L2 by about 2e-05, so no pointwise bound can be promised and the residual is what actually rejects missing work. The wider rtol on the BF16-output variants is load-bearing, not slack to reclaim.

What had to be renamed when nine modules became one file, and why each rename is a real difference rather than a merge artefact. Two entirely different kernels were both called `flash_attn_full_pj_hif8_kernel` and are now `flash_attn_full_pj_hif8_bf16_lag2_kernel` and `flash_attn_full_pj_hif8_fp16_lag1_kernel`. Three different (lookahead, slots) rings shared the names GROUP_LOOKAHEAD/GROUP_STAGE_SLOTS and are now DENSE_ (2/4), RING_ (3/5) and D256_ (2/4). Most dangerous of all, `HALF_M = TILE_M // 2` is the same line of text in every module but a different number in the D=256 pair, whose M tile is 64 rows -- so the d256 family carries D256_TILE_M and D256_HALF_M and a d256_ prefix on every masking helper that reads them.

`is_causal` on the d256 pair is a run-time kernel argument, not a build-time variant: the same emitted kernel serves `full_*` and `block32_*` cases, and the eight case pairs in main.py differ only in that one scalar. That is the cheapest available control for a mask -- same schedule, same tiling, same inputs, one switch.
do_not_copy_when: You want one attention kernel to read. This is nine of them plus a partial stage; pick the variant that matches your dtype and ABI and read only that one, or read a5_mha_fp16_bf16 for a single algorithm with three schedules instead.

You need a head dimension other than 128 or 256. The two widths are separate sources here with separate tile geometry -- the D=256 pair halves the M tile to 64 rows to pay for it -- and neither generalizes to a third width by changing a constant.

You want GQA or MQA without reading gqa_bf16 specifically. It is the only one of the nine whose K and V carry a different head count from Q; everything else in this folder assumes one KV head per query head, and a shared-KV layout changes the head mapping, the L1 residency and the partition together.

You are copying a tolerance. Every variant declares its own, for a numerical reason stated in main.py; the family-wide strictest rule is not safe for a BF16 output and the pv_stage rule is not safe for anything normalized.

entries.title: MLA attention, 512 + 64 score features
entries.formula: out = softmax((Q_nope @ K_nope^T + Q_rope @ K_rope^T) / sqrt(576)) @ V, query head h reading KV head h // 2; FP16 head-major [HQ*S, 512] and [HQ*S, 64] in, FP32 [HQ*S, 512] out
study_for: A score assembled from two separately shaped contractions. The 512-column non-rotary product and the 64-column rotary product are added before the maximum is taken, and the scale is 1/sqrt(576) over the combined width, not 1/sqrt(512). A kernel that computes one group and forgets the other still produces a plausible attention pattern -- this is what the relative-L2 bound in main.py exists to reject.

Head sharing without a shared-KV layout. Query head h reads KV head h // 2, and reference.py expresses that as `repeat_interleave(2, dim=0)` on the four KV heads. The `v_mode` case field is the control: `k_nope` gives V the same values as K_nope, `independent` draws it separately, which is what catches a kernel that reuses the K tile already on chip instead of loading V.

`QBuff(..., sync_depth=2)` in kernel.py separates physical slots from credits. Q, K and V keep four physical L1 slots so data survives across source timesteps, while autosync only issues a two-credit window because the local pipeline never has more than two in flight. Read this before assuming slot count and pipeline depth are the same number.

`accum_ws_valid` is a phase baton, not a data buffer: one initial token, one wait/set per online update, a final wait before normalization, one token handed to the next M tile, and one drain at the function tail. The score-reduction scratch is dead by the time P is cast, so kernel.py deliberately reuses those 16 KiB for P rather than placing a second P buffer above the A3 AIV stack boundary.
do_not_copy_when: Your geometry is not B1/HQ8/HKV4/512+64. Those five numbers are compiled into the kernel as constants -- the head mapping, the four 128-column D chunks and the UB budget all follow from them.
You need a causal mask. This body is dense over the whole KV range; the only masking is of tail columns and tail rows that do not exist.

You want the plain MHA shape. Everything specific here -- two feature groups, the 576 scale, the h // 2 mapping -- is overhead you would then have to remove; read examples/a2_vector first for the A2 vocabulary and a5_mha_fp16_bf16 for standard attention.

You are relying on the generic `CeilDiv` and modulo expansions. kernel.py spells the power-of-two divisions and bit-selected slot indices out by hand specifically to keep C220 from materializing signed-division correction temporaries in the A3 AIV scalar stack.

entries.title: SAGE decode attention over an int4/int8 KV cache
entries.formula: score = (int32(Q_i4 @ K_i4^T) * scale_q * scale_k + fp16(qm @ k_smooth^T)) / sqrt(128); out = int32(int8(127 * P) @ V_i8) * scale_v / 127 / rowsum, one query row per head, FP32 out plus FP32 rowmax and rowsum
study_for: Quantization the kernel never undoes. Q and K stay signed int4 all the way into the cube -- eight nibbles per int32 carrier -- the product accumulates in int32, and only then is it multiplied by the per-row and per-512-key-tile scales. The probabilities take the same route in reverse: scaled by 127, narrowed float32 -> float16 -> int8, contracted against int8 V in int32. reference.py reproduces every one of those boundaries in Torch rather than computing the float answer and rounding at the end, which is why the tolerance in main.py can be 1e-05 instead of a percent.

`unpack_signed_int4` and the `signed` input pattern are one idea in two files. The pattern forces a +7 into the low nibble and a -8 into the high nibble of every carrier family before anything else is drawn, because sign extension out of a packed int32 is exactly the kind of thing that works for the six middle values and fails at the two ends. The `source` pattern, which quantizes real floats, would almost never produce that pair.

Three published outputs, three different meanings. `out` is the attention row; `rowmax` and `rowsum` are the online softmax state captured before probability quantization, and they are what tell you whether a wrong `out` came from the softmax or from the PV contraction. main.py gives them their own comparison rule with no residual bound -- a relative L2 over a [BH, 1] tensor adds nothing to the elementwise bound.

The L1 V tail holds only `prev_valid_n` rows, and the comment in kernel.py says why that matters: functional simulation zero-initialises unread on-chip storage and silicon does not, so a contraction bound to the full tile instead of to the loaded extent passes under `--launcher sim` and returns garbage on a board. Bind the contraction to what was actually loaded.
do_not_copy_when: You need a query length above one. This is decode-only: TILE_M is 16 but exactly one row per head is live, only sub-block 0 publishes it, and the whole M axis is bookkeeping rather than work.
You need a causal mask or a prefill schedule. Attention here is non-causal over the whole KV cache, and the only masking is of tail columns past S2.

Your D is not 128 or your KV tile is not 512. CARRIER_D = 128 // 8 is the packed carrier width, TILES must equal ceil(S2 / 512), and the two-slot score/smoothed-score/P/PV workspaces were budgeted against that pair.
You want an unquantized attention demo. Almost everything in both files is the quantization path; read a5_mha_fp16_bf16 for the same algorithm without it.

entries.title: Streamed one-query decode attention, a 2x2 of four bodies
entries.formula: out[bh] = softmax(q @ k^T / sqrt(128)) @ v for one query row per batch-head, streamed in 128- or 256-key tiles with the probability tile rounded to FP16 before PV; FP16 [BH,1,128] q and [BH,S,128] k/v -> float32 [BH,1,128] out, S a multiple of the variant's key tile
study_for: A controlled 2x2: {ND, NZ} probability publication x {128, 256} streamed key width, four bodies that are otherwise the same and now four sections of one kernel.py. The entire structural difference between the `nd128.py` and `nz128.py` sections is the publish line — `l1p[...] <<= ub_p_half[...]` against `<<= ub_p_nz[...].nz()` — which is what makes the pair worth reading.

For an `L=1` decode row the score row IS a register list (`RegList(DT.float, BASES_128 // 64)`) and the online state is scalars read with `.single()`, so there is no per-step UB round trip for max and sum.
Single-owner publication done deliberately: `if GetSubBlockIdx() == 0` guards both the L1 P store and the final output store, so the peer sub-block runs the vector math and stores nothing.

The `M_src = src.shape[0]` rule for an NZ store is written down in the `nz128.py` section next to the call, with the oracle it came from named: the compact staging buffer has to be exactly `rows` tall, because its HEIGHT is the fractal-row stride the publish reads with. Declared eight rows tall it published seven fractal columns of memory nothing ever wrote.
do_not_copy_when: Your query block is more than one row. These bodies are row-specialised — the register list is the row.

Your key count is not a multiple of the variant's tile. There is no partial-tile path in any of the four: 128 or 256 keys arrive whole, and a tail is a wrong answer rather than a slow one. attention.a5_decode_fp8 is the one to read for a tail.

entries.title: Scaled E4M3 one-query decode attention
entries.formula: out[bh] = (E4M3(16 * exp(QK^T * scale_q * scale_k / sqrt(128) - rowmax)) @ V) * (scale_v / 16) / rowsum, one query row over S keys in 256-key tiles; E4M3 [BH,1,128] Q and [BH,S,128] K/V, float32 [BH,1,128] out
study_for: The other way to give a low-precision probability headroom: grep `P_SCALE` in kernel.py — a literal `regs * 16.0` on every P element, divided back out once at the end (`out_scale = scale_v / P_SCALE`). Put it beside the `-ln16` max bias in `attention.a5_pfa_hif8_metadata`, which reaches the same x16 with one `adds` on a scalar instead of a multiply over the tile.

`NEG_INF = -99999.0` rather than a true -inf, and the row state is initialised to it explicitly before the first tile — grep `init_row_state`, which also zeroes the whole accumulator instead of relying on the buffer being clean.

The row sum is accumulated in `get_p_and_max_sum_row` from the FP32 exponentials, before the same registers are multiplied by 16 and published as E4M3. Only the numerator ever passes through the low-precision carrier, so the denominator carries no quantization error at all.
do_not_copy_when: Your P is not being cast down. The scale exists to move P into the carrier's range; without the cast it is arithmetic you pay for and undo.
Your query block is more than one row. `rows = Var(1)`, the score row is a `RegList` and the online max and sum are read with `.single()`; a real query tile needs per-row reductions instead.

entries.title: Causal E5M2 flash attention with published row statistics
entries.formula: out = (E5M2(exp(Q @ K^T / sqrt(128) - rowmax)) @ V) / rowsum with top-left causal masking per head, 128x128 tiles; E5M2 [BH*S1,128] Q and [BH*S2,128] K/V -> float32 [BH*S1,128] out plus float32 [BH*S1] rowmax and rowsum, where rowsum is the FP32 probability sum taken before the cast
study_for: The causal boundary is rebuilt, never stored: `apply_causal_diagonal_sb0` fills a `MaskReg` from `cols.arange(...)` and one `compare`, then `select`s the masked lanes to `NEG_LARGE`. Nothing keeps a predicate in memory between tiles.

It is written twice, and the diff is the lesson: `_sb0` compares against `r + 1` and `_sb1` against `r + ROWS_PER_SB + 1`. Each vector sub-block owns a different 64-row band, so the diagonal offset is part of the body rather than a parameter — specialise per sub-block, do not branch inside the loop.
The N tail gets its own mask pass (`apply_n_tail_mask_multi`), kept separate from the diagonal so a tail tile pays for one and a diagonal tile for the other.
