`rowmax` and `rowsum` are public outputs, not debug state, and main.py compares them three orders of magnitude tighter than `out`. They are FP32 quantities defined before any E5M2 cast, so a wrong mask or a wrong score scale lands on rowmax instead of disappearing into the quantization noise of the result, and a denominator summed after the cast fails on rowsum alone.
do_not_copy_when: Your mask comes from runtime data rather than from the row index. `arange` + `compare` rebuilds a mask that is a FUNCTION of position; a data-dependent predicate needs the values on hand, and no unit in this gallery demonstrates that yet.

Your query tile is not 128 rows split 64/64 across the two vector sub-blocks. `ROWS_PER_SB = TILE_M // 2` is wired into both diagonal bodies, into the row-state addressing and into the eight-float head stride the row statistics are padded to so that each head and sub-block starts on a 32-byte GM transaction boundary — that padding is output-owned and sliced off by the host in main.py, and a copier who keeps the compact shape inherits the write conflict it exists to prevent.

entries.title: Standard MHA, three schedules
entries.formula: out = softmax(Q @ K^T * scale) @ V per batch and head, BSND, D=128, FP16 or BF16
study_for: Three schedules behind one kernel signature. `head_resident` keeps one head's K/V on chip and runs QK for the current item against a delayed PV for the previous one; `head_preload` widens the K/V pipeline to three slots and a 256-key tile for long causal prefill; `packed_decode` packs many one-query items into a single physical M128 tile. A case selects one by name and changes nothing else, so the three are directly comparable.

`weighted_partition` in kernel.py is host-only work: it partitions batch*head*query-group items across 28 cores by their causal key weight, elaborating the cut table as literals. It is neither a GM allocation nor a kernel argument, and it is a worked example of deciding a grid on the host instead of branching on the device.

How a demo stays runnable without a card: every full-shape case has a `model` counterpart shrunk around one named behaviour — a one-query tail, a head that must not be shared, an equal-but-not-aliased K/V pair, a zero input against a poisoned output. main.py runs the model cases under sim and skips the full ones with a reason.

The zero/nonzero pair. `model_resident_zero` feeds zeros into a NaN-poisoned output: the result is legitimately all zeros, so it only proves anything because `model_resident_nonzero` runs the identical signature with real values. A zero case alone cannot tell a correct kernel from one that writes nothing.
do_not_copy_when: You need GQA or MQA. Every head here owns independent K and V; a shared-KV layout changes the partition, the on-chip residency and the P publication together.
Your head dimension is not 128. D=128 is what makes one head's K/V tile fit the on-chip budget these three schedules were tiled against.
You want the smallest possible attention example. This is a complete kernel with tails, causal boundaries and three schedules — read a5_v8_cube_stage or a5_v8_p_stage for a single stage in isolation.

entries.title: MLA decode with split nope/rope scores
entries.formula: score = (Q_rope @ K_rope^T * scale_rope + Q_nope @ K_nope^T) / sqrt(576); out = E4M3(16 * exp(score - rowmax)) @ K_nope / rowsum, one query row per head over S keys in 256-key tiles; E4M3 [1,H,512] Q_nope and [1,H,64] Q_rope against [1,S,512] K_nope and [1,S,64] K_rope, float32 [1,H,512] out that keeps the 16x probability scale
study_for: The nope/rope split arrives as two separate matmuls and is combined in the VECTOR stage, not by concatenating features: grep `scale_add_qk_vf` in kernel.py — `(rope * scale_rope + nope) * SCALE`, where `scale_rope` is a per-batch runtime value read from GM. `SCALE` itself is `1/sqrt(Dn + Dr)`, taken over the combined width.
The E4M3 carriers are split too: `q_nope`/`k_nope` are Dn=512 wide and `q_rope`/`k_rope` are Dr=64, so the two products have very different K depths and are not interchangeable tiles.

K_nope is both the key and the value matrix: one `l1kn` tile feeds the QK matmul and then, transposed, the PV matmul of the same iteration (`matmul(l0cpv[...], l1p[...], l1kn[...].T, splitn=128)`). The tile is loaded once and its double-buffer slot is what ties the two stages' depths together.
do_not_copy_when: Your rope scale is a compile-time constant. Here it is a GM input per batch, and folding it into `SCALE` would change the ABI.

You need the normalized attention output. The 16x probability headroom is deliberately never divided back out — `E4M3(16 * P)` multiplies V while the denominator is the unscaled FP32 sum — so this kernel's result is 16 times the attention, by the source's convention, and the reference reproduces that rather than correcting it.

Your batch is larger than one or your key count is not a multiple of 256. The body addresses batch 0 (`q_nope[0, ...]`) and every key tile is a full BASES tile: there is no tail path here at all, unlike attention.a5_decode_fp8.

entries.title: Standard MLA, six schedules
entries.formula: out = softmax([q_nope|q_rope] @ [k_nope|k_rope]^T * scale) @ v over a single-head KV cache, Dn=512 or 448, Dr=64, FP16 or BF16, BSND and BNSD
study_for: Six schedules that all preserve the original 4-D ABI: no host packing, no GM workspace, no extra launch, no integer rescaling. That constraint is what shapes all six. `serial_nd` is the deliberately simple correctness baseline; `prefill_resident` holds one KV tile to avoid repeated online-state updates; `decode_preload` and `online_prefetch` are the M128 pipelines; `online_paired` groups core intervals by even item ceilings; `decode_splitkv` is the one that breaks the no-workspace rule on purpose.

`decode_splitkv` is the one to read for a cross-core merge: FP32 partials into private GM workspace, an all-Vector barrier, then a stable log-sum-exp merge in the SAME kernel, with producer M64 groups and merge row groups distributed independently. The inputs stay read-only throughout.

`serial_nd` documents a padding obligation that is easy to miss: eight logical query heads share one physical M16 cube tile, so every Q and P row that M16 reads has to be initialised — including the rows belonging to the vector participant that does no work.

The four `serial_*` cases are controls, not extra coverage. Each runs `serial_nd` at exactly the shape of a teaching case, so when an optimised schedule disagrees with the oracle you can tell whether the shape or the schedule is at fault. Use `--variant` to run one schedule across every case that selects it.

MLA's KV cache has one head: `k_nope`, `k_rope` and `v` carry 1 where the query carries Nq, and `v` holds `k_nope`'s own values in separate storage. That absorbed-V form is the layout, not an accident of the input generator.
do_not_copy_when: You are taking `serial_nd` as a performance model. It is a correctness baseline and says so; the other five exist because it is not fast.

entries.title: BF16 prefill attention, two shardings of one mathematics
entries.formula: out = softmax(Q @ K^T / sqrt(128)) @ V per batch, computed as score^T = K @ Q^T; BF16 Q[B*MQ,128], K/V[B*N,128] and out[B*MQ,128], FP32 score, exponentials and online state, BF16 P before the PV matmul
study_for: Read the transposition first, because every other choice here follows from it. The scores are computed as `score^T = K @ Q^T`, so `softmax_t_vf` works on [key=128, query=64]: keys are rows, queries are lanes, and the per-query maximum is four independent partial-max chains down the 128 key rows with a tree-combine. There is no cross-lane reduction anywhere in this kernel. If your scores are untransposed, the reduction is the part that does not transfer and you need a real cross-lane reduce instead.

The `flat.py` section of kernel.py is the clearest statement of software pipelining across tile boundaries in this tree: fusing the (M-tile, K-tile) loops into ONE linear `step` loop lets the lag-2 pipeline carry across M-tile boundaries, so M-tile B's QK ramp overlaps M-tile A's PV drain and the per-M-tile ramp/drain bubbles -- 2 QK-only and 2 PV-only trips each -- disappear. It also states the price: `k_tiles >= 2`, and the per-M-tile state has to be double-buffered by M-tile parity so A's drain and B's ramp do not share it.
What does NOT get double-buffered is as informative: `rmax` stays single, because only stage 1 touches it and stage 1 is strictly serial in `step`.

The `flat` and `fd` bodies are the same mathematics over two different shardings -- M-tiles only versus the flat (m_tile, k_tile) stream-K grid -- with the FD merge of two FP32 partial states and its explicit ties-away BF16 cast at the end. main.py runs the same four shapes through both, so the pair is directly comparable, and the two entrypoints share one copy of the geometry and the softmax/accumulate/finalise VFs because the two source modules defined them identically.
do_not_copy_when: You have one K-tile per M-tile. The lag-2 fusion needs at least two, and the parity double-buffering needs adjacent M-tiles to differ in parity -- which is why every `flat` case here has N > 128.

More than two cores can own one query tile in the `fd` sharding. The merge reads exactly two workspace slots per split tile, so a `block_dim` that cuts one M tile three ways, or that puts two interior boundaries in the same tile, merges the wrong pair without complaining. Each case names a block_dim that satisfies the precondition; it is not a free knob.
Your head dimension is not 128. D=128 is wired into both bodies as TILE_M/TILE_N=128 and two 64-lane FP32 register chunks per output row, and is not a parameter despite being a kernel argument.

entries.title: All-HiFloat8 PFA: four publication bodies and five precision studies
entries.formula: out(B*MQ,128) bf16 = sum_n hif8(exp(s - m)) @ V / sum(exp(s - m)), s = Q K^T / sqrt(128) over uint8 HiFloat8 Q(B*MQ,128) and K/V(B*N,128); nz and v8 bias the exponent by ln16 so P and its denominator both carry a factor of 16, while v9 and study_v2/study_v4 hold s and the online state in FP16
study_for: The variant list is the lesson index. `nd` publishes P key-major in ND; `nz` builds NZ directly in UB with a four-key deinterleave at physical stride 33; `v8` groups three physical 128-key score tiles under one maximum update so three P beats accumulate into a single L0C PV result; `v9` exports the score to FP16 through two SINGLE drains with a FixP19 scale. Four answers to "how does P get from the vector side back to the cube".

The five `study_*` bodies are the other axis: ONE schedule held fixed while two things move. V1/V2 take the FixP19 scale at the fixpipe drain and V3/V4 take it in the vector function; V1/V3 keep FP32 state and V2/V4 keep FP16. The fifth, `study_v3_splitn`, moves neither -- it is V3's arithmetic through a single SPLITN fixpipe bridge instead of two SINGLE ones, which is why it needs scale 1.0 (SPLITN cannot requantize). All five are complete attention kernels with their own cases; the thing that is not a kernel is the `_nocv` companion each of them has, whose cube-to-vector mutexes are replaced by a no-op so a missing handoff shows up as a wrong value rather than a hang.

`v8`'s credit ring holds six ordered P0/P1/P2 beats, and `v9` retires exactly three beats for every final-group length from 1 to 384 -- including a phase-only P2 that uses the same event pair as a real one. That is how a variable-length tail keeps a fixed-shape pipeline honest, and the nine `v9_*` boundary cases (N = 1, 127, 128, 129, 255, 256, 257, 383, 897) are the enumeration of it.
do_not_copy_when: You are picking a winner from the archived campaigns. The HQ8/S4099 and HQ40/S9360 numbers quoted in the v8 and v9 module headers are source history and select nothing; nothing here is a speed claim.
You need the `nocv` bodies to be correct. They are diagnostics whose synchronisation is removed on purpose, no case runs them, and running one and getting a number proves nothing.

Your last key group can be shorter than 129 keys and you are copying `v8`. Its source domain is 129..384 keys in the final group, because a zero second tile does not retire its event beat. `v9` is the variant that handles every positive tail, and this demo no longer has the host-side guard that used to reject the short case before launching it.

entries.title: Host-scheduled all-HiFloat8 GQA prefill
entries.formula: out = softmax(Q @ K^T / sqrt(128)) @ V over one shared KV head, computed as score^T = K @ Q^T with P = 16*exp(s - rowmax) published in HiFloat8; HiFloat8 Q[M,128], K[N,128] and V[N,128] in uint8 carriers, BF16 out[M,128], FP32 state merged across host-owned key intervals
study_for: How to keep a probability inside a narrow float without paying for it per element: grep `LN16` in kernel.py. Biasing the running max by `-ln16` once makes `expsub` return `16 * exp(s - m)` for free, so the x16 threads through the row sum and the accumulator and cancels in the output, while the stored running max stays the true one. Compare `attention.a5_decode_fp8`, which spends a `muls` on every P element to get the same headroom.

The nz4 constant block records why each number is what it is, including the negatives: `FRAC_STRIDE4` is 33, not 32, because one pad row per NZ fractal dodges a bank conflict -- the same +1 shows up in every NZ P publication in this directory tree; `UNROLL4 = 2` says higher unroll gave no speedup; and `_DEINT_U8` is a flip-if-the-board-rejects-hif8 escape hatch that is off.

Both L0C drains, in production form: `DualMode.SPLITN` for the transposed score tile, because after `score^T = K @ Q^T` the query rows are its N axis, and `DualMode.SPLITM` for the PV result, where they are the M axis again -- grep both, the second is commented `each AIV its 64 query rows`. The rule is "split whichever axis carries the query rows", not "always SPLITM".

Only the HOST metadata generator is target-aware. The kernel reads `GetCubeNum()` and its own row of the per-core table, so the same body runs on a 32-core and a 28-core part as long as the generator emits that many rows -- see the comment block above `FA_NF`, and `reference.schedule`, which is that generator.

entries.title: Seven HiFloat8 studies: four P publications, three synchronisation protocols
entries.formula: out(B*MQ,128) bf16 = sum_n hif8(exp(s - m)) @ V / sum(exp(s - m)), s = Q K^T / sqrt(128) over uint8 HiFloat8 Q(B*MQ,128) and K/V(B*N,128); the seven variants compute the same function and differ only in how P reaches L1 and how the two sides synchronise
study_for: `main.py`'s `KERNELS` map with `CASES` is the comparison table: seven variants over one unscaled-HiFloat8 body, each running the same six geometries, so what differs between any two rows is only what the variant's name says. Under sim all forty-two agree with the independent oracle to max_abs_diff 0.0 — the seven really do compute the same numbers.

Four ways to get a HiFloat8 P tile into L1 in NZ, differing only in the softmax `@vf` pair passed to the shared body: `nz1` MULTI4 squeeze then a masked strided store at pitch 129; `nz2` the same store fed by a uint8 gather at indices 0,4,...,252; `nz3` squeeze plus an even-byte zero interleave, a LOWHALF predicate and a uint16 scatter (the M10-031 ABI correction, whose zero byte is built as uint8 and reinterpreted because C310 has no HiFloat8 scalar broadcast); `nz4` the four-key native HiFloat8 deinterleave into four 32-key slabs at pitch 33, through `_full_nz4_body`.

Three synchronisation shapes over ONE schedule, which is the rarer comparison: `nd_fused` uses end-pipe-only C/V mutexes; `nd_mutexse` passes `_pv_se()` / `_p_se()`, the same mutexes with their start pipes declared equal to their end pipes; `nd_splitevent` keeps the plain mutexes, keeps `auto_sync`, and adds `ev_qk` and `ev_pv`, two `SEvent(Pipe.M, Pipe.FIX)`, inside the cube side. Same numbers, three protocols.

The construction that makes those comparisons cheap: every body takes its mutexes as arguments (`_cv_normal()`, `_pv_normal()`, `_p_normal()` and their `_se` twins), and the NZ bodies take their softmax pair as arguments too, so a variant is a different call and not a forked body.

You want a ranking. The unit records what each variant does, not which one won, and it makes no speed claim.

Your P operand is not the 64-key-wide HiFloat8 tile these publications assume. The pitch-129 and pitch-33 carriers, the MULTI4 squeeze, and the uint16 scatter's even-data/even-predicate lane rule are properties of that layout, not of the softmax in front of them.

entries.title: Per-task GM metadata attention: the meta8 and meta11 ABIs

Scalar geometry that lives in GM has to be loaded explicitly. Every field goes through `Var.GetValueFrom` on a one-element GM view (`meta[0:1, i:i+1]`), not through an implicit read — all-integer tensor indexing is not part of the GM-view syntax.

The two-owner flash-decoding merge. The same comment carries the cost of the alternative on this shape: an fp32 -> fp32 dual destination is a cheap fixpipe, and the fp16 SINGLE-mode path it replaced measured +82us.

A forward-only L1 ring for the P tile: grep `vec_ready` and `wait_vec` -- raw flags on MTE3/MTE1 with no backward edge, which the comment marks as intra-block rather than S/FFTS. A mutex would have added a return edge this handoff does not need.

Flash-decoding partials reach the workspace only at an m-block boundary, into a head or tail slot chosen by which end of the key range this core owns: grep `fd_accum`, `head_ws`, `tail_ws`. The slot numbers are not computed on the device -- they arrive in fa_meta, which `reference.schedule` builds.

`schedule` offers four core splits and the four declared cases select only three of them: `staggered`, `whole_query` and `even`. The fourth, `fia`, is a recorded 28-core cost-aware split taken from a real run, and it is live code on a live branch — it simply has no case. entries.title: Presence-table sparse mask
entries.formula: prob_t[k,q] = exp(score_t[k,q] - rowmax[q]) if query q selects key k else 0; present_t[k,q] = 1.0 or 0.0 for that same selection; denom[q] = sum_k prob_t[k,q]; float32 [1024,64] transposed scores, int32 [64,64] selected columns (1024 means no key) and float32 [1,64] running maximum -> float32 [1024,64] prob_t and present_t plus float32 [1,64] denom
study_for: A mask that is not known until the data arrives, kept as ordinary data and rebuilt with one `compare` instead of stored as a predicate. Grep `reg_to_ub_scatter` in kernel.py: a marker is scattered to each selected key column, and the read side compares it back. The table costs 32 times the bytes of packed predicate bits, which is why it covers a chunk of key columns and is rebuilt per chunk. Take the trade for the reason it was actually made — recompute beats resident on this device, measured in the production kernel this pattern comes from as 722 us of rebuild against 161 us of cube work — and not for the reason it warns against: the backend prints `vf.mask_to_ub` and `vf.ub_to_mask` (library `262d6d6`), so a spilled predicate is possible and still the worse design.

Generation markers instead of clearing. The value written is the chunk's generation number, so a residue from an earlier chunk carries an earlier number and `EQ` misses it — a cleared table with no clearing pass. Grep `EPOCHS` and `_clear_presence`: the real clear runs only when the counter wraps.

One unsigned subtract and one `< CHUNK` classify every index slot at once — below this chunk (wrapped to something enormous), above it, and the reserved padding value. The result goes straight into `reg_to_ub_scatter(..., mask=live)`; the shape this replaced spent two `select`s rewriting rejected indices to a scratch column, and dropping the mask is an out-of-range store rather than a slower kernel. `GUARD = 1` is the spare table row hedging the same edge, and it was measured rather than asserted: with `GUARD = 0` the board returns a bit-identical answer, so at this size the row is not load-bearing. The simulator could not have settled that — it applies the mask first and range-checks only the surviving lanes.

The masked-write table in one body: `expsub(numerator, row, ceiling, live)` zeroes the lanes it turns off, which IS the masking — no second pass zeroes the absent keys, and the row sum accumulates them with no further guard. A masked `dup` three lines below builds the exact 0/1 `present_t` output the same way. Read it with the library's `docs/api/mask-write-semantics.md`.

Why an exactly-compared output earns its place. This unit publishes the rebuilt predicate as `present_t` and main.py compares it EXACTLY rather than folding it into the exponential's tolerance — and that is what made library M10-077 findable: the PyPTO Pro printer was dropping the mask from a masked scalar `vf.dup`, so `present_t` came back 1.0 in all 65536 cells while `prob_t`, whose mask the printer did carry, was right to one ULP. Under a tolerance the wrong predicate would have been a wrong number nobody questioned. Publish the thing you are asserting.
do_not_copy_when: You are taking the chunk width. 128 key columns is narrow on purpose, so that eight rebuilds fit a small unit and the generation counter wraps once. A real attention kernel has cube work between rebuilds, so each rebuild is its own `@vf` entry, and the entry plus its tail barrier puts the floor nearer 512 columns.
You need both vector sub-blocks. This is one core, one sub-block, no `dual_mode` anywhere; for that axis read attention.a5_v8_cube_stage.

You want the smallest table. This one is `uint32` so that the marker register and the score register share a lane width and one predicate serves both. A 16-bit table halves the bytes and then owes a `mask_pack`, because a b16 `compare` writes different physical predicate bits than a b32 consumer reads.

You want a performance figure. Nothing in this folder was timed: the geometry was chosen to make the failure modes observable, not to match a production shape, and the 722/161 us pair quoted above belongs to the production kernel rather than to this stage.

Put V there and the free fires while the store is still reading the tile; `--launcher pipesim` reports that as a WAR hazard.

entries.title: V8 P stage: exp, fused rescale, strided publication

Determinism around a strided store. The P stores skip one 32-byte block per fractal column (`block 32 + 33 i`) and the tail writes three rows only, so the kernel zeroes the tiles first. That is what makes every published byte defined, and it is what lets this demo compare whole physical carriers instead of only the live rows — run `--case padding_poison`, which fills the incoming carrier with 0xA5, and watch the answer not move.

Comparing against a SET of admissible answers instead of one. The device's native `exp` is within one measured FP32 ULP of a correctly rounded exp; at a HiFloat8 quantization boundary that one ULP picks the neighbouring code. `reference_candidates` propagates the interval through the same ties-away conversion, and `compare_one_of` prints how many elements actually had two admissible codes. Under sim that number is 0 for every P tile except `padding_poison`'s `p1`, where it is 1 of 8448 — the whole reason the mode exists is that single element.
A legitimate single-owner stage: one public output tensor, so the peer vector sub-block stays idle by design rather than by oversight.

Your P operand is not in the packed 33-row NZ carrier. The skipped block per fractal column and the three-row tail are properties of that layout, not of the arithmetic.

entries.title: NSA sliding-window KV compression
entries.formula: out[i,n,:] = sum_{j<L} input[win_start[i]+j, n, :] * weight[j, n], accumulated in fp32 in the upstream ReduceBlock fold order and rounded once to the storage dtype with ties away from zero; a batch of sequence length S contributes floor((S-L)/d)+1 whole windows when S >= L and none otherwise; fp16 or bf16 [T,N,D] input with [L,N] weight and an int32 [Tc] table of window starts -> [Tc,N,D] output
study_for: Two rounding decisions that a tolerance would have hidden, and how each was caught. The single narrowing cast breaks ties AWAY FROM ZERO (AscendC CAST_ROUND, `RoundMode.AWAY_FROM_ZERO`), where `torch.Tensor.to` breaks them to even -- 14 of 200000 random fp16 values disagree, every one an exact tie. And fp32 addition is not associative, so the ORDER of the L-term sum is observable too: grep `fold_plan` in kernel.py and `reduction_order` in reference.py for the upstream ReduceBlock order, which folds the non-power-of-two remainder onto the front and then halves the stride. Both are stated twice, once per file, and the demo's exact comparison is what holds them together.

What an upstream oracle is worth. The rounding mode was recovered by reading sources; the reduction order was not. Running the real vendor operator on an A2 card (`torch_npu.npu_nsa_compress`) against this reference disagreed on 4 of 9216 elements in ut_a1_fp16 -- and recomputing those four windows three ways showed all four matching the tree and none matching a serial sum. Nothing below hardware would have found it: sim, pipesim and the card all agreed with the wrong reference, because the kernel had the same wrong order.

Why the fold is a loop over `(stride, count)` and not the expression tree it is equivalent to. A depth-first walk of the tree needs only log2(L) live registers and no staging buffer, and it emits correctly -- then bisheng spills it, because the walk unrolls into straight-line code: measured at L = 32, 35 vector slots and 8992 bytes against a 6144-byte VF stack. Staging the products in UB and folding them with small device loops keeps the emitted body near 120 lines for every L. A static Python container is what makes the strides compile-time without any device division, which would otherwise have pulled in the integer-cast supplement.

A hazard the simulator does not model. The folds read what the products loop wrote and each fold reads the one before it, and a UB store inside a `@vf` is not visible to a later load without `vf_barrier(VfPipe.STORE, VfPipe.LOAD)`. Without those barriers sim and pipesim both stayed green on every case while the card returned every case wrong. Grep `vf_barrier`: one after the staging loop, one after each fold.

Sizing the backing a whole-register access needs, which is not one rule. M10-088 makes a LANES-wide footprint real however few columns are live, so `_geometry` gives the two read-only tiles spare ROWS -- an overrunning read lands in the next row, which is written later or is spare -- and gives the staged products a LANES-aligned row PITCH instead, because the folds read and write them in place and an overrunning store would clobber a row that is still live. The first shape is what the emit gate forces: a wider tile with a narrower transfer into it is refused as `dma.gm_to_ub.pad: a partial transfer into a tile window stacks two validshapes`, which is also why `head_tile` returns a DIVISOR of N so every group is the same constant width.

How a data-dependent output length reaches a backend that specialises per scalar valuation. The upstream output row count is computed from the VALUES of an int64 prefix sum (its infershape reads them). Grep `window_starts` in reference.py: the host expands that into one absolute row index per output token and the device takes an int32 table, so no int64 reaches the card. The justification is a boundary rather than convenience -- the upstream's own tiling already reads actSeqLen to derive kvStartTokenIdx and PerCoreStartOutputOffset. `start.GetValueFrom(...)` then feeds only an address: every tile dimension stays a compile-time integer, which is the line RFC-0013 draws and attention.a5_pfa_hif8_task_metadata records the other side of.

Where the time went, measured, and what each measurement changed. One Ascend950PR card, the board launcher's profiler (device-side Task Duration, not host wall time -- the harness round trip is ~7.6 s per launch and identical for a 0.01 MB case and a 2.9 MB one), on a 302 MB input because this part's L2 holds 112 MiB and every demo shape fits in it several times over. block_dim 8 -> 28 was 3.48x; fusing the first reduction fold into the products loop was 1.10x and halved the staged tile; double-buffering the window and the output row was another 1.92x (1034 -> 535 us at L == stride). The re-read of an overlapped window, which looked like the obvious target, measured free and was never written: the L = 2*stride shape requests 1.91x the bytes for 1.24x the time at identical UNIQUE traffic, because the re-read rows are still in L2. The per-pipe ratios are what said which to do: before double buffering nothing exceeded 0.53, so it was dependency-bound rather than pipe-bound; after, `aiv_mte2` 0.955 leads at L == stride and `aiv_vec` 0.986 leads at L = 2*stride, which is the crossover the timing already implied.

Two defects the simulator cannot see, and the case each one needed. (1) The weight splat writes one whole register per head, which covers a head of 64 columns or fewer by overrunning into the next -- and covers only the first 64 columns of a wider one. Every case here had D <= 64 except the D = 256 one, and that shape routes to the sub-head group, so the wide whole-head path had no case at all: reaching a constraint's extreme value is not the same as reaching the code path that value takes. `wide_head_multi_chunk` is the case that does. (2) The pipeline's prefetch, left unguarded, wrote the next window into `xa` after the last pair of a column group had already consumed it -- a write with no reader, whose only successor is the next group's prologue write to the same tile. On the card the stale one won and the first output row of every group after the first came out of the previous group's columns. sim, pipesim, PyPTO-Pro and CCE all called it correct, and CCE failing the same way is what proved it was ours; `many_head_groups` is the only case with a second group for the first one's epilogue to race.
do_not_copy_when: You need the overlapped regime to be traffic-optimal on a part with a smaller L2, or with a stride so much smaller than the window that the halo no longer fits. On this part it measured free (see the last study_for entry), so the halo scheme -- a core owning a contiguous run of output tokens and loading it once with an L-stride halo -- was deliberately not written. That is a measured choice, not an unexamined limit, and the measurement is what you would have to redo rather than the reasoning.

Your head count is prime and your head is wide. `column_tile` prefers the widest DIVISOR of N whose group fits, then falls back to a slice of one head, so the geometry is always uniform and always a compile-time constant -- a ragged last group would need the partial transfer into a wider tile that the emit gate refuses. The cost lands on a shape like N = 7 with a head too wide to pair up: one head per group, one transfer per head per token. Correct, and more transfers than a ragged split would need.

You want the upstream ABI. This takes [T, N*D] and [1, L*N] views plus a host-built int32 window table; it does not take layout strings, an int64 actSeqLen, actSeqLenType, or anything but the TND layout the upstream itself restricts to.

You want a number for a different part, a different launch width or a different backend. Everything above is one card, PyPTO-Pro, the block_dim each case names -- and a `block_dim` tuned for one card is not tuned for another, with nothing here to notice that for you. CCE appears only as a control that adjudicates a failure; it is not what this demo delivers.

entries.title: Masked scale over a tiled vector
entries.formula: y = (x * mask) * scale, float32, n in [1, 16385], tiles of 128 or 8192 elements
study_for: One algorithm, two devices. The kernel body is a plain function; `build_kernel(device)` applies `ascriptor.a2.kernel` or `ascriptor.a3.kernel` to it at call time. That is how to support both without duplicating source or flipping a process-global switch — and why a device change needs a fresh process, since importing a facade selects device state the module cache will not give back.

The tail is the whole point of the case list: n = 1, 63, 64, 65, 257, 515, 129 and 8193. `valid = Min(tile_len, n - n0)` and the `[0:1, 0:valid]` windows on every load, compute and store are what make those work; a kernel that computes a full tile and stores a windowed one passes n = 64 and fails n = 65.

Cores that get no work. With block_dim = 4 and n = 129 only two cores own a tile; `tile_begin`/`tile_end` collapse to an empty range for the others and they must exit through `auto_sync()` cleanly rather than store anything.

Why the mask contains zeros and the destination starts as NaN: a masked lane's correct answer is 0.0, which is exactly what an unwritten lane would look like if the output buffer were zeroed. Poisoning it with NaN is what makes 'did not write' distinguishable from 'wrote a zero'.
do_not_copy_when: You need a dtype other than float32. The UB double buffers are sized [1, 8192] float32; another dtype changes the tile capacity and the tail arithmetic with it.
Your work does not partition by whole tiles. Cores here take a contiguous run of tiles, so the split is only correct because every tile except the last is full.
You are on A5. This uses the A2 tensor-vector vocabulary (`mul`, `muls` over UB tiles), not the A5 `@vf` register surface — read examples/axpy for that.

entries.title: AXPY on one vector register
entries.formula: o = float32(float32(2 * x) + y) over a contiguous float32 [1, 64]
study_for: The smallest complete A5 demo: one `@vf` body, three UB tensors, one `auto_sync()` scope. Read this first to see what the four files of a demo folder are for before opening anything larger.

A `Reg` is a whole 64-lane vector register, not a scalar: `xr <<= x_ub[0]` loads the entire row and `muls`/`add` write one register each. The kernel has no loop because the shape is exactly one register wide.

Bitwise comparison is a claim about the arithmetic, not a default: multiplying by exactly 2.0 and adding in float32 is what the independent Torch reference also does, with no reduction and no fusion, so any difference is a defect.
do_not_copy_when: You need more than one core. This kernel has no partitioning: every lane of the output belongs to one vector core, and a second core would race.
Your shape is not exactly 64 lanes. There is no tail handling here — [1, 63] and [1, 65] are both wrong, not slow.

entries.title: Delta Rule backward, five stages
entries.formula: d(q, k, v, beta) of the chunked ungated delta rule, L=64 chunk, D=128, BF16 inputs with FP32 accumulation
study_for: A five-launch pipeline as one demo. main.py's `execute` is the whole composition: each stage's destinations are allocated NaN-poisoned by the caller, handed to OpExec with `seed_outputs=True`, and passed on to the next stage. Read it before writing any multi-kernel project — the ordering and the tensor plumbing are the design, not an implementation detail.

`--stages` compares all eleven intermediates against `reference_stages`, so a wrong final gradient can be traced to the launch that produced it. Without it you only learn that d_key is wrong, not which of the five stages made it wrong.

Why the default runs the whole sequence and never a stage alone: on-chip storage is not cleared between launches, so a stage can be exact in isolation and wrong once a predecessor has run on the same core, reading that predecessor's accumulator leftovers. The functional simulator cannot represent this at all — it gives each launch fresh, poisoned on-chip storage.

Two vf helpers here started life with the same name in two stage modules and are not the same function: `cast_l_rows_float_to_bf16_nz_vf` and `cast_l_rows_float_to_bf16_nz_barrier_vf` differ by one `vf_barrier(STORE, LOAD)`. Separate modules hid that; one file makes it visible.
do_not_copy_when: You want the gated variant. This is the ungated delta rule: it is gdn_bwd evaluated at g == 0, so every exp(g_cumsum) factor is 1 and the intra-chunk decay mask is a constant strict-lower keep. Read gdn_bwd if you need the gate.
Your chunk length is not 64 or your head dimension is not 128. The L=64 / D=128 pair is what the NZ fractal layouts, the 16-row BF16 C0 and the on-chip budget of all five stages were built around.
You only need the forward. delta_rule_fwd is a shorter read and the backward consumes forward state (wu_attn, k_cumdecay, state history) that this demo has to prepare for itself in reference.py.

entries.title: Delta Rule forward, four stages
entries.formula: o[c] = q[c] @ S + tril(q[c] @ k[c]^T) @ v_new[c] with v_new[c] = u[c] - w[c] @ S and S <- S + k[c]^T @ v_new[c], where (w, u) = (I + (k k^T * beta) tril_strict)^-1 applied to (k*beta, v*beta); ungated, L=64 chunk, D=128, BF16 tensors and state with FP32 beta, zero initial state
study_for: A four-launch pipeline as one demo. main.py's `execute` is the whole composition: preprocess -> triangular inverse -> recompute W/U -> fused chunk recurrence, with every destination allocated NaN-poisoned by the caller and handed to OpExec with `seed_outputs=True`. The one destination that is real zeros rather than poison is the initial state, because the first chunk reads it before anything writes it.

`--stages` is not just extra printing: it swaps `recurrence_saved_kernel` in for `sub2_kernel`, because that is the variant which publishes the state and v_new histories, and it launches the standalone `sub1_kernel` score leaf that the production recurrence fuses rather than launching. Without that leaf the fused causal-mask epilogue is only ever checked against itself.

One stage, three source kernels. `INVERSE_KERNELS` holds the block inverse and the two Neumann variants, and a case exercises each. The Neumann cases are the only ones whose residual against the fp32 reference is not exactly zero under the simulator (about 2e-3 relative L2, 4.9e-4 on `wu_attn_bf16`), which is what bf16 cube operands and bf16 intermediate publishes cost in an inverse.

`attn_causal_keep_vf` and `score_causal_keep_vf` are the same body under two names: the standalone leaf's and the fused recurrence's. They are deliberately not shared, so that editing the fused path cannot quietly edit the leaf the fused path is measured against.
do_not_copy_when: You want the gated variant. This is the ungated delta rule: it is gdn_fwd evaluated at g == 0, so every exp(g_cumsum) factor is 1 and the intra-chunk decay mask is a constant causal keep. Read gdn_fwd if you need the gate.
Your chunk length is not 64 or your head dimension is not 128. There is no L or D tail path here at all; an incomplete B*H*C core assignment is handled by bounded loops, but a partial tile is not.
You need a trainable or otherwise nonzero initial state. Only the zero-initial-state path exists, and the production backward has no initial-state gradient to pair with one.

You are carrying this preprocess precision into a backward fixture. This forward applies beta after `key @ key.T` in fp32 (`delta-forward-post-mm-beta/1`); delta_rule_bwd's saved-state fixture rounds `key*beta` into a bf16 cube operand before that matmul. The two are not interchangeable and swapping them moves the third digit.

entries.title: GDN backward, five stages
entries.formula: d(q, k, v, beta, g) of the chunked gated delta rule with per-token log gate g, intra-chunk keep exp(g_cumsum_i - g_cumsum_j) under the causal mask, L=64 chunk, D=128, BF16 [B,H,C,64,128] inputs with FP32 accumulation and FP32 gradients
study_for: What a per-token gate costs a backward that already exists. Against delta_rule_bwd this adds one input (`g_cumsum`), one materialised [64,64] `decay_mask`, one output (`d_g`), and a gradient path that does not look like the others: `finalize_grads` in reference.py assembles d_g_cumsum from d_g_core + d_g_wu, folds the decay-mask gradient in as `(d_decay_mask * decay_mask).sum(-1) - (d_decay_mask * decay_mask).sum(-2)` — the row/column asymmetry is the i-j in the exponent — and only then runs `reverse_cumsum` to turn d_g_cumsum back into d_g.

finalize's gate reduction is batched four BHC rows at a time, so its d_g operands (`d_g_core`, `d_g_wu`, both masked decay gradients) and its d_g destination are flattened to [BHC, ...] while every other tensor stays [B,H,C,...], and four constant GM operands — `selector_rows`, `neg_selector_rows`, `eye`, `reverse_tril` — carry that batching and the reverse-causal keep. The `partition_tail` case is BHC=6 precisely because 6 is not a multiple of 4: it is the only case that runs the partial batch-tile path.

inverse_preprocess reuses the retired L0C tmp ring for d_attn after its FIX copy, and its vector stage captures each complete input row in registers before writing the results back in place — d_attn becomes d_score, decay_mask becomes d_decay, preprocess_score becomes the masked d_decay. The Cube-to-Vector credit is only returned on MTE3 after those final reads. That is 32 KiB of L0C and 40 KiB of UB bought with a read-before-write ordering, and it is the part that breaks first if you reorder the vector stage.

Two vf helpers here started life with the same name in two stage modules and are not the same function: `cast_l_rows_float_to_bf16_nz_vf` (scan_local) and `cast_l_rows_float_to_bf16_nz_barrier_vf` (inverse_preprocess) differ by a single trailing `vf_barrier(VfPipe.STORE, VfPipe.LOAD)`. Separate modules hid that; one file makes it visible.
do_not_copy_when: You do not need the gate. delta_rule_bwd is this unit evaluated at g == 0: no g_cumsum operand, no materialised decay_mask, no d_g output, and a constant strict-lower keep instead of exp(g_cumsum_i - g_cumsum_j). It is the shorter read and the better starting point.

Your chunk length is not 64 or your head dimension is not 128. L=64 / D=128 is fixed and there is no L or D tail path: the NZ fractal staging, the 16-row BF16 C0 and every on-chip budget in the five stages were sized around that pair. Only the BHC count is allowed a tail.

You need a nonzero initial state or a gradient with respect to it. This backward supports the zero-initial-state path only and d_initial_state is not in its ABI, so the boundary term you would need has no producer here.

You want the forward's preprocessing convention. This backward preserves the source's ordering, rounding `key * beta` into the BF16 cube operand before `key @ key.T`; forward-v2 applies FP32 beta after that matmul. The two saved-state generators are not bitwise interchangeable and the reference here models the backward's, not the forward's.

entries.title: GDN forward, five stages plus saved state
entries.formula: o[c] = (q[c] @ S) * exp(g_cum[c]) + attn[c] @ v_new[c] with S <- S*exp(g_last) + (k[c]*exp(g_last - g_cum[c]))^T @ v_new[c], chunked at L=64, D=128, BF16 tensors and state with FP32 gates, zero initial state
study_for: A five-launch pipeline whose forward also publishes the backward's saved state. main.py's `execute` is the whole composition: preprocess -> strict triangular inverse -> recompute WU -> scores -> recurrence, with every destination allocated NaN-poisoned by the caller and handed to OpExec with `seed_outputs=True`. The seams are fp32 (`g_cumsum`, `decay_mask`, `strict_lower`) up to the bf16 WU handoff, and bf16 after it.

The recurrent tail exists as two kernels, `gdn_recurrent_plain` and `gdn_recurrent_saved`, running the same recurrence with and without the four history stores. Their entry names differ so their generated artifacts cannot collide, and `--stages` launches both: a disagreement between them is the saved kernel's extra stores disturbing its own state, which a single-kernel check could not tell from an error in the shared maths.

`make_kexp_vf` and `make_kexp_saved_vf` are the same weighted-key arithmetic, but the saved one additionally writes the fp32 `exp_delta` row and an ND copy of the bf16 weighted key beside the NZ one. They started life under one name in two stage modules, which is exactly the kind of near-duplicate that separate files hide and one file makes visible.

`tril_inverse64_v2_strict_bf16_kernel` keeps two slots per L1/L0C ring and reuses its first-use inputs (`a10/a21/a31/a32`) as temporary and product storage once their MTE1 reads have retired. It needs 32 Cube and 30 Vec mutex IDs including the default L0A/L0B scratch, and holds explicit M-to-FIX and FIX-to-MTE1 events around the publish because of the PyPTO Acc-to-Mat pipe selection gap (A5-UP-039).
do_not_copy_when: You need a trainable or otherwise nonzero initial state. Only the zero-initial-state path is implemented, and the backward this forward feeds has no `d_initial_state` to match.
Your chunk length is not 64 or your head dimension is not 128. There is no L or D tail path here at all: the producers partition whole 64x128 tiles and the recurrent kernels partition whole BH pairs.

You are copying the preprocess precision into a backward. This forward computes bf16 `key @ key.T` with fp32 accumulation and applies beta afterwards in fp32; delta_rule_bwd and gdn_bwd round `key*beta` into the bf16 cube operand before the matmul. The two conventions disagree at the third digit and must not be swapped silently.
You want the ungated delta rule. Set `g == 0` and every `exp(g_cumsum)` factor collapses to 1 and the decay mask becomes a constant causal keep; delta_rule_fwd is that case written without the gate.

entries.title: KDA backward, nine stages
entries.formula: d(q, k, v, g, beta, h0) of chunked Kimi Delta Attention with a per-(token, channel) log2 gate and a chunk-local inverse-triangular solve, L=64 chunk, K=V=128, BF16 [B,T,H,128] queries/keys and [B,T,HV,128] values in and out, FP32 accumulation
study_for: How to contract a decay-weighted pairwise term without ever building the decay matrix. `finalize_pre` writes `q_scaled = q * exp2(g_cumsum - g_last)` and `kg = k * exp2(g_last - g_cumsum)` -- reciprocal scalings, one of which reaches 1e25 while the other stays under 1 -- so `finalize_pair` can do the whole O(L^2) intra-chunk pairing as four plain cube matmuls and `finalize_post` multiplies the reciprocal scale straight back in. It is the central trick of this backward and it costs something real: see the note beside `finalize_pair.qk_right` in main.py's TOLERANCE for what an intermediate spanning 1e13 orders of magnitude does to an elementwise comparison.

What the nine launches are for. Read the section banners in kernel.py in order: `finalize_pair` has no vector code at all (four matmuls, 56 lines), while `inverse_epilogue`, `finalize_pre`, `finalize_post` and `finalize_reduce` have no cube at all. The split is the cube/vector alternation, not an arbitrary decomposition -- each boundary is a point where the work changes pipe, and `main.py`'s `execute` is the only place the whole ABI between them is written down.

Two references that disagree on purpose, and a demo that runs both. `reference` differentiates the unrounded fp32 forward with autograd; `reference_stages` models the bf16 and fp32 seams the kernels actually use. That is why `--stages` measures the kernels and the default run measures the algorithm, and why `dk` and `dg` are the only outputs with relaxed residual ceilings (0.15 and 0.25): the saved cumulative gate is stored bf16, so a log2 value can move by up to 0.25 before `exp2` is applied, which lands directly on a multiplicative derivative.

Where an all-bf16 ABI still keeps fp32 in GM. Every public input, every saved forward cache and every public gradient here is bf16, with exactly two exceptions, and both are accumulation points: `inverse_epilogue` emits `dbeta` as fp32 [B,T,HV], and `finalize_post` emits `dq_hv`/`dk_hv` as fp32 [B,HV,C,64,128] which `finalize_reduce` sums over the HV group before rounding to bf16. Rounding either one early loses the group sum.
do_not_copy_when: Your gate is a natural exponential. KDA's gate is base 2 throughout: `g` is scaled by 1/ln(2) into `g_cumsum` and every decay is `exp2`. A stage lifted into an `exp()` pipeline gives a plausible wrong answer instead of failing, which is what the `gentle_decay` case exists to catch -- a shallow decay makes the disagreement visible where a steep one buries it.

Your chunk length is not 64 or K/V is not 128, or T is not a multiple of 64. There is no partial-chunk path. The authored scope is L=64, K=V=128, T=C*64, and the [B,HV,C,64,128] to [B,HV,T,128] view punning that main.py's `execute` does between finalize_pre, finalize_pair and finalize_post is only free because those shapes are the same bytes.

You want the delta rule without a per-channel gate. KDA's gate is per (token, channel) -- a full [B,T,HV,128] tensor, not one value per token. gdn_bwd is the per-token-gate version and delta_rule_bwd is the ungated one; both are much shorter reads and neither needs this unit's nine launches.

You want to lift one kernel out and use it alone. Nothing here is standalone: `finalize_pair` consumes M_qk/M_base/M_beta and the three scaled products exactly as `finalize_pre` laid them out, `inverse_dakk_fused` reads D_tri through a [B,HV,T,64] view of a [B,HV,C,64,64] tensor, and `inverse_mm`'s third output is negated by the caller rather than by the kernel. Those conventions live in main.py's `execute`, and a kernel taken out of it drops them silently.

entries.title: KDA forward, five stages
entries.formula: o[t] = q[t]*K^-0.5 @ S with S <- S*exp(g[t]) + beta[t]*k[t] (v[t] - k[t]^T S), chunked at L=64, K=V=128, BF16 q/k/v/o with FP32 gates, strict score and state
study_for: A five-launch pipeline as one demo. main.py's `execute` is the whole composition: `chunked` permutes the public token-major tensors into the BHCLK/BHVCLK layout the kernels index, every destination is allocated NaN-poisoned by the caller and handed to OpExec with `seed_outputs=True`, and the seams between stages are fp32 `g` and `strict` but bf16 `Aqk/Akk/w/u/kg`.

The two checking modes, and why one is not enough. `execute` chains the five kernels; `execute_stages` hands each of them the reference's own upstream values instead. Only the first can catch a stage that is exact alone and wrong after a predecessor has run on the same core; only the second can say which of the five launches produced a wrong `o`.

The WY precision boundary is real, not an artefact of the reference. `kda_sub3_wy_kernel` rounds `Akk*beta_col` and `k*g` to bf16 *before* the cube products, so `reference_stages` does the same; an fp32-throughout reference disagrees with the kernel at the third digit and the disagreement is the kernel being right.

`tril_inverse64_v2_strict_bf16_kernel` inverts `(I - strict)` on a 16x16 block schedule with two slots per L1/L0C ring, reusing each first-use input (`a10/a21/a31/a32`) as temporary storage after its MTE1 read. It needs 32 Cube and 30 Vec mutex IDs including the default L0A/L0B scratch, and keeps explicit M-to-FIX and FIX-to-MTE1 events around the publish because of the PyPTO Acc-to-Mat pipe selection gap (A5-UP-039).
do_not_copy_when: Your chunk length is not 64 or K/V is not 128. The fused tail exploits the fact that at V=128 both 64-wide value tiles of every assigned (B,HV) pair always exist, so it carries no per-tile bounds branch; partial chunks, K or V tails, fp16 and L=32 are outside what this kernel answers for.
You need variable length. This is the fixed-length path only: no `cu_seqlens`, no `cp_context`, no `safe_gate`, no gate fusion and no `state_v_first`.

You are writing the backward. kda_bwd has a different saved-state ABI — bf16 log2 cumulative gates, bf16 state and nine saved tensors — and this forward's fp32 linear gates and internally retained `h`/`v_new` are not that cache. Do not present one as the other.
You want the ungated delta rule. Set `g == 0` here and every `exp(cumsum(g_raw))` factor collapses to 1; delta_rule_fwd is that case written without the gate and is a much shorter read.

entries.title: A late P reader and the buffer lifetime it forces
entries.formula: y = (relu(x@w1 * 0.25 + 0.5).half() @ w2) + x@w1, FP16 operands, FP32 accumulation, 32-row tiles
study_for: The one idea: `p` has TWO readers at different depths. The activation reads it immediately; the residual add reads it again after the second matmul has run. Its slot's lifetime is set by the LAST reader, not the first. Give it `h`'s lifetime — whose last reader is the second matmul — and the three-slot lookahead overwrites `p` one tile early.

Two schedules, one formula, so the comparison is controlled. `late_reader_serial` finishes a tile before starting the next; `late_reader_pipeline` starts the next tile's matmul while this tile's vector work runs. They must produce bit-identical output, and the cases run the pipelined ring at 1, 3 and 7 tiles so it wraps zero, one and two times.

Run it under `--launcher pipesim`, not just `sim`. The functional simulator gives each launch its own storage and will happily accept a lifetime that the real pipeline would violate; the pipe model is the one that knows when a slot is reused and reports the hazard.

Why the comparison is exact and not a tolerance: the inputs are dyadic (multiples of 1/32 and 1/16 in a bounded range), so every FP32 product and sum is exact. The single deliberate FP16 materialisation of the activation is the only rounding, and both sides do it identically.

entries.formula: alternating matmul and vector stages over the pattern string, FP16 operands, FP32 accumulation, FP16 between stages, 32-row tiles
study_for: A controlled comparison, which is what makes it teachable: the four schedules of one graph compute the same function, so if `pipeline` disagrees with `serial` the schedule is the only thing that can have caused it. Start with CVC, read `cvc_serial` and `cvc_pipeline` side by side, then look at what `resident` adds on top.

Every kernel is written out in full instead of being built by a Python loop over stages. That is deliberate: a stage delay, a slot index and an edge's owner are visible in the source of the kernel that has them, and nothing is decided at device-loop time. Twenty near-identical kernels is the price of being able to diff two of them.

Sizes are chosen against the slot ring, not for coverage: 1, 2, 3, 5 and 7 tiles make it wrap zero, once and several times. A schedule bug that needs a wrap is invisible at one tile and obvious at seven.

`pipeline` is the only schedule that also runs on two cores, at the three sizes where the ring wraps. It is the schedule whose correctness depends on how items are split across cores, so that is where the split and the delay can interact.

The per-tile mark in column 0 of `x`. A lost drain, a wrong delayed index and a stale resident slot all move rows between tiles; without the mark those show up as a plausible number, with it they show up as the wrong tile's value.

You want a tuned kernel. These are correctness demonstrations of scheduling shapes; nothing here is measured, and `resident` is not automatically faster than `serial` at these sizes.

You need more than three weights or a graph that is not a simple alternation. The pattern string is walked stage by stage against w0, w1, w2 — a branch or a shared stage is outside what these twenty kernels express.
